7966bf89c0ac8347: BERLIN: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Thursday that he was open to having Germany join a next-generation fighter jet project, after the collapse of a Franco-German warplane programme.
Britain, Italy and Japan are working on the "Global Combat Air Programme" (GCAP), which aims to replace the Eurofighter Typhoon and Mitsubishi F-2 jets currently used by those countries.
Germany's competing next-generation fighter jet project with France and Spain - the "Future Combat Air System" (FCAS) - fell apart in June amid bickering between the companies involved.
During a visit to Berlin, Burnham said he had told Chancellor Friedrich Merz about Britain's "openness to Germany joining GCAP" during discussions earlier in the day.
Burnham said he hoped to work with Italy and Japan "in the coming period" on having them join as well.
Merz, standing alongside Burnham, did not comment on the issue.

The FCAS project foundered after French aerospace group Dassault demanded greater control over the initiative, a push that ruffled feathers in Berlin and at the defence branch of Airbus, which is based in Germany.
Both France and Germany had prioritised keeping local industry involved in cutting-edge defence projects as part of the programme.
That could pose an obstacle for adding Germany to the GCAP programme, since major firms in all three countries such as BAE Systems, Leonardo and Mitsubishi have already divided up much of the work.
Swedish aerospace firm Saab has also been mentioned as a potential partner for Germany and Airbus in building a next-generation fighter.

French and German officials have publicly maintained that other parts of the FCAS project, such as networked combat computer systems and a swarm of drones that would accompany the fighter, will continue.
And an eight-company consortium including Airbus has pitched Berlin on building the next-generation jet themselves, in place of FCAS.

773ef63da905c60c: The use of phishing emails as a means of stealing information or implanting damaging malware dates back to the mid-1990s. Although almost as old as the Internet, it remains the instrument of choice for threat actors wanting to pose as trusted organizations or individuals for the purposes of corporate infiltration. In fact its use is on the rise: according to the most recent figures from the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), some 26 percent of all cybercrime complaints filed with them are now phishing-related. The bad news doesn’t stop there. Phishing is mutating in alarming new ways, raising all sorts of difficult questions for defenders and placing email security at a tricky inflection point. AI has for years been a useful tool in the hands of the cybercriminal. But the advent of Generative AI (GenAI) is proving a cyber game changer, transforming phishing from a widespread but easily identifiable nuisance into a lethal precision instrument. Aspiring phishers have historically been hindered by various constraints. Their attempts at chummy authenticity have often been undermined by easy-to-spot mistakes and amateurish formatting – blemishes that traditional email security is good at picking up. Personalised attacks have also been hard to launch at any kind of scale. GenAI sweeps all technical, linguistic, and operational restrictions aside by automating sophistication. Attackers no longer have to choose between individually targeted “spear phishing” which takes much effort to coordinate, and large-scale attacks that lack finesse. Now, with minimal expertise and at low cost, they can hit thousands of victims with minutely tailored phishes at the press of a button. Today’s Large Language Models (LLMs) generate polished and contextual text in any language, backing it with realistic brand graphics and convincing web addresses. At a stroke, Gen AI has democratized this type of crime, putting it in reach of anyone capable of the most elementary research. “Thanks to AI, the historic signals that exposed a phishing email – poor grammar, misspelt words – are now ironed out and replaced with perfect language,” notes Dave Baggett, SVP Cybersecurity with software developer Kaseya. “These emails can be highly targeted with the help of AI. You can create an email that pinpoints, say, a pharma company by using authentic terminology. It’s an incredibly powerful tool for the bad guys.” And let’s not forget that where this new AI-enabled phishing is successful, it is not just a single unwary employee whose data is at risk. Once past the perimeter, a bad actor can get to work burrowing into the cloud and SaaS platforms that now underpin global commerce and communications. All in all, it’s easy to understand how losses from phishing attacks have gone up 274 percent in the last couple of years, according to the FBI. This new email security landscape is an alarming development for corporate IT bosses, and also for MSPs who must be super wary on behalf of customers who don’t have the expertise to pick up attacks at this pitch of sophistication on their own. AI is for the good guys too It’s not all bad news on the email security front line. As threat actors have been perfecting their use of GenAI, defenders have been developing AI-driven counter solutions in parallel. Where old school protection relied on spotting the kind of anomalies that GenAI has now ironed out, newer solutions are geared more towards contextual analysis. They are not so much trying to spot clumsy typos and dodgy attachments as model an attacker’s intent before damage is done. Today defenders can use AI to analyze subtle patterns that are in tune with the layered structure of modern phishing campaigns. The aim is to determine whether a message aligns with expected behavioral patterns. This level of finesse is made necessary by the insidious nature of modern phishing which means that technically clean email messages, in other words ones that are free of malware-loaded attachments or booby-trapped links, can still contain malicious potential. Modern cybercriminals often bypass automated security filters by the simple means of exploiting human psychology and trusted infrastructure. Social engineering, supercharged by GenAI, can be a sharper sword than a malware payload. A phish will often seek to impersonate a boss or a colleague using a plain text email. Attackers can set GenAI to scour LinkedIn, looking for people who have just started new jobs. Green employees are more vulnerable to a phish that looks like an email from a new superior they haven’t got to know yet. Once trust is established, what will typically follow is a demand for, say, an urgent wire transfer, or a casual request for payroll details or passwords. Attackers can develop a relationship over multiple emails to “groom” the victim before striking. Traditional filters see nothing suspicious. Spotting this sort of attack demands a smarter grade of tool. “Since attackers are relying on manipulation of fallible individuals, security must now support them at the moment where wrong decisions can be made,” says Baggett. “Good email security will replace generic warnings with easily digestible context about why a message might be risky and advice about the need for further verification.” Where once an inbox was a passive delivery channel, says Baggett, it is now an active layer of risk mitigation, tooled up to stamp out a phishing attempt before it escalates into account compromise and devastating financial loss. A huge asymmetry The good guys are fighting back. But as Baggett points out, there remains a huge asymmetry between bad actor and defender: “Attackers can use LLMs, basically for free, to create perfect phishing templates,” he says. “On the other hand, if defenders took every inbound email and put it through a frontier LLM model, that’s about 100x too expensive. We just can’t use the same tools at the criminals.” One option for defenders is to use smaller, more specialized models, distilled from larger ones. A compact model could be tuned, for example, to the sentiment or meaning of each phrase in an email, and set to pick up a threatening tone or a favor being asked. Where chunky LLMs just cost too much, another choice might be to run a subset of the overall inbound mail through a big model: “Admins can be given a way to run particular mails through a frontier LLM,” says Baggett. “That model will have been trained to understand certain critical aspects of email security.” Better use could be made of pre-LLM tools such as computer vision, which can help process, analyze and understand visual data like digital images and videos. Other ancillary tools that could enrich the defensive mix include sender analysis to look into the origin and authenticity of an email message, and linked-content inspection that can examine an email in depth without triggering any embedded threats. There are some reasons to hope for a safer future as AI technology evolves. As inference becomes smarter and models get better, it should become possible to run a higher percentage of emails through a large scale LLM, believes Baggett. This, however, may not be achievable for some years. There’s also the possibility of using LLMs not just to spot potentially malicious emails but also to analyze the settings and admin controls of existing security tools. In this way, the knowledge required to use the tools to best effect becomes much less. “Security tools can be complex and feature hundreds of settings,” points out Baggett. “Some require expertise that our customers don’t have. There are a number of things we believe tools should be doing to help defenders, for example reduce alert fatigue.” The criminal fraternity may, of course, also find ways to harness better tools for new purposes. At the moment, most attacks are conceived and designed by humans. But ultimately, this job may be taken over by agentic models able to figure out new tactics for themselves. Machines may soon be able to plan and supervise attacks at scale. Great tools, available now Luckily defenders don’t have to sit back and be at the mercy of future developments. There are some great tools available today that help them even up the odds and cut the complexity from checking email. INKY Smart Insights, for example, uses GenAI to reduce a lengthy manual email investigation to a few seconds of automated triage. For the purposes of hard-pressed administrators it can turn a mess of technical email evidence into a plain-language verdict and enable the creation of cogent reports. Along with Kaseya Intelligence it can support decision-making across the broader security environment. “Smart Insights will identify problems and give a narrative explanation of its reasoning,” enthuses Baggett. “It will do that in a way that’s not overly technical, making the tool valuable to someone who doesn’t have expertise in email security.” The hard-pressed MSP, for example, can leverage Smart Insights to provide key information for their customers in an abbreviated and digestible format. In short, it allows them to enjoy the sophistication of LLMs but without adding hugely to their overheads. The war on GenAI-powered phishing is far from won. But so long as defenders can understand the potential of the smart tools at their disposal, they have a fighting chance of keeping the bad guys at bay and essential channels of communication safe. 5cd9ee2507606018: "Forget It" was the name of a small computer program never thought to be needed, which will nonetheless go down in history along with its author, Margaret Hamilton, the American software engineer who died on September 30, aged 90. Hamilton led development of the onboard flight software for Apollo's command and lunar modules, helping astronauts reach the Moon in 1969. Among her early jobs after joining the MIT Instrumentation Laboratory in 1965 was to write the software for the Apollo abort procedure. "Everybody said that was never going to happen, [so they said] 'Oh well, good. We'll give this one to Margaret because she's a beginner,'" she told the Computer History Museum. However, an unmanned flight did abort, raising Hamilton's standing within the team. "It went to [run] this program I had written, which I named Forget It. All of a sudden, I became an overnight expert," she said. Hamilton was born in Paoli, Indiana. Moving with her family to Michigan, she graduated from high school in 1954. She studied mathematics at the University of Michigan and Earlham College, where she graduated in 1958 with a minor in philosophy. She planned to pursue graduate studies and an academic career, but decided to go to Boston in 1959 with her husband, who was studying law at Harvard. She got a job at MIT with Edward Lorenz – who went on to pioneer chaos theory – and programmed the LGP-30 and DEC's PDP-1 computers for weather forecasting. She worked on other projects at MIT, including aerospace systems, before hearing of the Apollo missions in 1965. She immediately applied to join the MIT team supporting them. She initially wrote software for uncrewed Apollo missions, later leading development of flight software for the crewed program. The team's software played a crucial role in the first lunar landing as the Apollo 11 module approached the Moon's surface in 1969. During the final minutes of descent, the guidance computer raised several unexpected alarms, leading the astronauts to question whether it was safe to land. The alarms showed "executive overflows," meaning the system could not complete all its tasks. Hamilton had also pressed for safeguards against operator error. Her daughter, four years old at the time, crashed a command-module simulation by activating a pre-launch program during a simulated flight. Hamilton proposed protection against that mistake, but was initially overruled because astronauts were considered unlikely to make it. An astronaut subsequently did so during Apollo 8, prompting changes to the software. For Apollo 11, the software's restart protection allowed essential landing tasks to continue despite the overload. Computer engineer Jack Garman advised guidance officer Steve Bales that the alarms did not require an abort. "We're go on that alarm," Bales confirmed. The crew made it safely to the Moon's surface and later returned to Earth. The overload was traced to unwanted inputs from the rendezvous radar system. While working on the Apollo missions, Hamilton began to call herself a "software engineer" because writing code was not taken as seriously as other engineering disciplines. The term is now standard. She also features in an iconic photograph, standing beside a stack of her team's Apollo software listings almost as tall as she was. Following the Apollo missions, she founded and co-founded a number of technology companies focused on fault-tolerant software. She created the Development Before the Fact (DBTF) methodology to prevent errors early on, along with the Universal Systems Language (USL) for systems design. In 2016, President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Computing pioneer Grace Hopper received the same honor posthumously. The White House described Hamilton as a mathematician and computer scientist who contributed to concepts of asynchronous software, priority scheduling and priority displays, and human-in-the-loop decision capability, which set the foundation for modern, ultra-reliable software design and engineering. Hamilton's legacy is a reminder to design for the mistakes users supposedly won't make – and the failures no one expects. She is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons, four great-grandchildren, and three siblings, according to MIT. ®

7359c0168c4c2b1d: PETALING JAYA: Semua sekolah di empat negeri serta Kuala Lumpur dan Putrajaya ditutup mulai esok berikutan jerebu.
Menteri Pendidikan Fadhlina Sidek mengumumkan semua sekolah di Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Melaka dan Johor ditutup; manakala di Pahang semua sekolah di daerah Rompin ditutup.

Pihak sekolah juga perlu memastikan kelangsungan proses pengajaran dan pembelajaran dengan menggunakan kaedah bersesuaian, mengambil kira kemampuan, akses serta keperluan murid dan kesiapsiagaan guru.

f4f2e6f4d721163f: PETALING JAYA: Education minister Fadhlina Sidek has announced that all educational institutions in Selangor, Melaka, Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya will close tomorrow due to the worsening haze.
Fadhlina said that in Pahang, only schools in Rompin will be closed.
She said schools in Perlis, Perak, Penang, Sabah, Sarawak and Labuan will operate as usual.
Earlier today, the education department in Negeri Sembilan announced that all schools in the state would be closed tomorrow, while schools in Johor are closed today and tomorrow.

This evening, the education ministry said schools in areas that record air pollutant index (API) readings of more than 180 are to close tomorrow, while schools in areas that record APIs of more than 150 for three consecutive days will close from Oct 12.
API readings of between zero and 50 are categorised as good, 51 to 100 as moderate, 101 to 200 as unhealthy, 201 to 300 as very unhealthy, and 301 and above as hazardous.
At 10pm, a total of 36 areas recorded unhealthy API readings, with Seremban in Negeri Sembilan and Segamat, Johor, topping the list at 188.

afaa6403611628c8: My Decoder guest today is Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, and we’re discussing the new wave of consumer-friendly AI agents.

If you’ve been paying attention to this space, you know AI enthusiasts have been using agents for a minute now — homebrew OpenClaw setups led to a surge in Mac Mini sales earlier this year. But the launch of Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, and xAI’s Grok bot has brought easy to use agents to millions.

Muse and Dots have had the highest-profile product launches, and they’re fascinating to pit against each other. Both Meta and OpenAI have decided to pitch these agents to mainstream users and businesses in the form of cute, animated mascots.
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

These can do everything from the boring — restaurant reservations and inbox triage — to more sophisticated tasks. In OpenAI’s cases, the company is even offering “specialist” Dots for marketing, legal work, and accounting.

Muse, notably, is free, while Dots are not. So you’ll hear Hayden and me get into why Meta, which still doesn’t have a frontier model of its own, might have a meaningful edge here because it’s so much better at making and distributing consumer products.

There’s also a huge Decoder-style tension wrapped up in the agent race: a conversation about what AI is good at today, what it still can’t do, and then the privacy and security implications of handing over your credit card information, your email inbox, and other sensitive hard drive data to an AI that might be able to do things for you without even requiring an app or a phone in your hand.
That might be the future of all computing, but it’s not at all clear if most people want to hand over the data to make it happen.
Okay: The Verge’s Hayden Field on Muse, Dots, and trusting AI agents. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Hayden Field, you’re the senior AI reporter here at The Verge. Welcome back to Decoder.
Thanks so much.

I’m excited to talk to you. This time there isn’t any wild interpersonal drama. No one’s feelings have been hurt. I would say Elon Musk tried to hurt some feelings and didn’t get there. Alexandr Wang from Meta has maybe been taking some shots, but none of the Real Housewives stuff we usually end up talking about when you’re on the show.
It’s been a bit of a pause in the soap opera antics for now, which I’m really grateful for.
Yeah, just some good old-fashioned product competition in the marketplace. Let’s see who wins and loses, and maybe everything will kill us all in the end. But, for now, cute mascots.

There’s a lot going on. Let’s start at the start. Hayden, you were at OpenAI DevDay in San Francisco. The company announced Dots, which is their new agent platform with a cute mascot. That happened just a few weeks after Meta Connect, at which the company was all in on Muse, their agent platform with an adorable mascot.
Tell us about the state of the industry right now. Everyone’s very excited about agents. What’s going on?

It’s funny to me because I’ve been covering agents for so long. I remember that in 2022, it was the year of ideation — that’s what tech leaders called it, referring to agents. They were just ideating. They were thinking about what it could look like. There were a lot of references to Jarvis from the Marvel Universe.

They called 2023 the year of deployment: “Let’s try things, let’s deploy and learn more about what’s failing.” Which meant pretty much all of them were failing at the time. Then we had 2024 and 2025. They didn’t have any names for those years, but agents were still pretty bad, as we saw.

2026 seems, to me, like the year of the beginnings of actually useful AI agents for the consumer, like always-on autonomous agents. Obviously, OpenAI was the start of all of this. But what’s interesting to me is that one man, Peter Steinberger, was able to create an actually useful AI agent for the consumer with OpenClaw — an always-on tool, despite its privacy flaws. It had a lot of privacy and security issues.

But it was an agent that was useful enough that people still wanted to use it anyway and try to find ways around these privacy issues that it was having. That inspired these companies to say, “If one man can do this over the course of one weekend, we’ve really been slacking. We have to get it together.”

OpenAI hired that guy, and now we have Dots. Meta, of course, was working on its own version of this and put it out sooner with Muse. They’re basically both always-on, autonomous AI agents that these companies are peddling as a way to be your personal assistant in a lot of ways.

The idea is to use them for booking flights, booking dinner reservations, buying gifts for people, but not only that. Some of them, Dots in particular, are kind of going further to be your work personal assistant and we’ll get into that in a minute.
But this is where OpenAI and Meta are warring right now. They’re trying to present these two AI agents as a little bit different from each other, even though they’re essentially the same.
Just broadly speaking, to define some terms, we’re gonna keep saying “agent,” and what we mean here is an AI model wrapped in a harness that lets it use a computer.
Right. The way that I describe AI agents usually is an AI tool that can complete multi-step complex tasks on your behalf without you hand-holding it the whole time.

I was a personal assistant in one of my first jobs in New York, so I would’ve gotten fired if every time my boss asked me to book a flight for her, I said, “What time? Also, what’s your SkyMiles number? Also, what’s your loyalty number again, for this other thing? Oh, do you want me to try to get you first class?”

They want you to have common sense and just book the flight. This is what they’re pitching these AI agents as — things that can work on their own mental kind of scratchpad in the background and not ask you every single time there’s a step. They can complete multi-step processes in the background, doing their own reasoning, and then present you with a completed task.

That’s the big idea. Just to say it clearly, both Muse and Dots come out of the OpenClaw lineage, which is a technical approach to building an agent, right? There are a lot of different ways you might be able to accomplish “It’ll remember your SkyMiles number and book you a flight.” But the way everyone’s going at it now is the idea of a harness around a model. That was the big innovation in OpenClaw, and the computer OpenClaw was using was often your own Mac Mini on your own network using a wide-open browser with your own data, which is where a lot of their security problems came from.

It’s the same model with Muse, only it’s a little Linux computer that Meta’s giving you in the cloud. It’s the same model with Dots, although the way ChatGPT is set up with Codex is very complicated, and that computer could be in a lot of different places.

But this notion that what you really need is a computer with a browser and some harness is gonna direct a model to do a bunch of stuff for you using that computer, that’s what we’ve landed on today, and it just seems to be the default winning model.
Right.
Are all of these things just riffs on OpenClaw? Are they the same as OpenClaw?

You could say that. They’re different technically. Meta keeps saying, “We did build this from scratch, but it was inspired by OpenClaw.” There are a lot of similarities there, but they did say that they built it from scratch. Then, of course, OpenAI hired the creator of OpenClaw, so there’s probably a lot of similarities there as well for Dots.

The reason I wanted to stay there for one second is that I think it’s important to identify the fundamental technical approach that is happening with these agents, because there’s a lot of different ways it could have gone, and the whole industry has picked this approach. What you need is a web browser, a harness, and a model that can go use that web browser.

What’s really interesting to me is that Meta has done a really good job on top of that fundamental model of making a cute consumer product. Meta is good at consumer products. Obviously, Instagram and Facebook and the rest are undeniably good consumer products. People really like them.

For all of Meta’s failings in VR, I always thought the Meta Quest has been a great consumer product. You take it out of the box, it helps you use it, you can have fun with it right away. Whereas Dots seems like it’s kind of made for software engineers, but you can also plan a wedding in it.
I’m wondering if that’s how you see it. That one is an enterprise product with a little consumer gloss on it, and then Meta obviously is just a dead-ahead consumer product.

What’s different here is that OpenAI needs money a lot more than Meta needs money. The products are honestly pretty similar, it seems like. The difference is that OpenAI is marketing it to be an enterprise-friendly product a lot more than Meta is. Muse is just a consumer-facing product.

Meta is happy with that. The goal is to make Muse as easy to use as humanly possible. One-tap downloading, just putting it in your face literally everywhere. Even when I went to my Instagram profile the other day, there was a pop-up for using Muse. They’re trying to make it free, accessible, and super easy to broaden the audience.

They want anyone to be able to just use it with one click and get used to it. They’re trying to flood the market with AI agents and make it normal and have their own ChatGPT moment, if you will, for AI agents. They want Muse to be that. Now, with OpenAI, they’re still marketing it as a consumer-facing product. When you’re using ChatGPT, if you have the right subscription, it’s right there.

It says, “Use your Dot to do this, that, and the other.” They really want you to go for it as a consumer, as long as you’re paying. This is for their $100 to $200 a month subscription tier, unlike Meta. That’s why there’s a huge difference here. For OpenAI, it seems like they don’t have the money to just front-load all of this and say, “Use it for free. No problem. We’ll catch up with you later.”

OpenAI wants this to be a money-making product, and that’s why they’re marketing it to the enterprise. They talked a lot about privacy to try to set it apart from Meta’s Muse. They talked a lot about what you could do with this as a knowledge worker, whether you worked in marketing, graphic design, software engineering, product, and tons of different industries. They gave examples of how you could use this as an assistant, as a coworker. Sam Altman even referred to it as like a “chief of staff.” He didn’t want it to be just an assistant. He wanted it to be your chief of staff.

Something else that I thought was interesting is that Sam Altman seemed to subtly dig at Meta on stage a few times during DevDay. One of the times he said, “Look, I don’t want this to be just something that’s used to book flights or plan things with friends and look at your calendar. I want this to go beyond that and to really do knowledge worker tasks, things that you in your industry would need a niche assistant to perform.”

That’s why they also introduced specialist Dots that are good at marketing, legal analysis, and things like that. They’re really going for the enterprise angle here, but I think it’s also because they need money ahead of their IPO, obviously.

Yeah, the revenue piece — that it’s only for paid customers at their higher tiers — is really interesting. OpenAI’s tiers are very confusing, but it’s $100 and up, and that’s just going to keep a lot of people from using Dots at first.

The flip side of that is OpenAI does have a lot of customers who are paying them a lot of money, and if they can get those customers to start using Dots, then those customers will be on their agent platforms and maybe you will get some lock-in.

You’ve given those agents a lot of data. They’re part of your workflows, and that might solve the problem I think we’ve seen all the frontier labs have, where a new model comes out and it’s slightly better than the competitor model, and everyone switches for six months, and the next new model comes out and everyone switches back.
Is there some thought that these agent platforms create lock-in — create actual loyalty on top of just the models being better?

Yes. They’re basically hoping that they can build a moat with their users for these things. If Meta and Google already have super easy integrations with all of each company’s existing tools and services, they can easily keep you there.

For example, I have an Apple iPhone, but I use almost exclusively Google apps. So if Google had an AI agent that I was using every day, it would be a little tough for me to switch. That’s what they’re hoping for here.

Meta is hoping that they can get you so into the Muse ecosystem that it would be tough for you to switch, and maybe one day you do have to pay. With OpenAI, they’re trying to get you locked into their ecosystem right away. Even though you have to pay up front, they’re thinking, “We have integrations with almost every tool and service. Maybe it’s not as good as the company that owns that tool and service, but we have the variety and the breadth.”

They’re going for quantity here. One of their employees told me that. They said, “Maybe our Gmail integration, for example, isn’t gonna be as good as Google’s, but we have a Gmail integration and an Outlook integration and X, Y, and Z.” They’re going for just the power of choice and the fact that power users will hopefully stay in this moat.

It’s funny, you mentioned Google. Google announced an agent called Gemini Spark. We should mention that SpaceXAI, the very coherent company that everyone understands, has an agent called Grok Bot, which it is promoting heavily. People seem to like it. It was built by the Cursor team, which SpaceX acquired.
There’s a lot of this going around, but it seems like Meta really got there first with a consumer product that people could understand.
Obviously, Grok Bot and Dots are much more enterprise-focused, coding-focused. Why was Meta able to get there first?

From all my reporting on Meta, they’ve been behind in AI for a while, and Mark Zuckerberg basically said, “We’ve got to lock in and make a product that people are gonna use on our platforms.” Alexandr Wang apparently was more looking to create a frontier model that was gonna compete with the other leading frontier models.

He says, “We have to think long-term. We have to think superintelligence.” But Zuckerberg says, “No, we gotta think cold hard cash, as in getting people to use stuff on our own platform.” Where they met in the middle was an AI agent that people would use on the Meta platforms, but that still represented a huge step forward, they hoped, for AI systems and what they could do in the everyday world.

This is a fascinating dynamic in that Meta still doesn’t have a frontier model. I don’t think anyone at Meta is claiming that the Muse Spark model competes at the frontier of GPT-6, but their product is better, and certainly they have a massive distribution advantage. They don’t have to pay for advertising on Meta platforms, and OpenAI does, and certainly they have a consumer design advantage. Meta is just better at consumer products.

Does that change how you feel about the dynamics of competition in AI at all? For so long, it’s just been about the capabilities at the frontier, but now it’s a little bit about marketing. It’s a little bit about product design.

You don’t have the best model, but you made a consumer agent product and you connected it to giving everybody a computer in the cloud, so now it can actually do things for you, and its frontier capability is actually not the important thing. It’s its capability.

I think the more money and power you have at one of these companies, the more get mentally farther away from what the average consumer wants. Let’s say the average consumer does want an AI agent, which many of them don’t, as we know.

But let’s say they do. If they do, they’re going to want it to be free or cheap, and they are going to want it to be safe to use without creeping them out too much. They’re willing to deal with a little bit of creepiness in order for it to be free, but not too much. Meta’s Muse has made headlines about some of its privacy issues that have gotten a little bit above that comfort level for some users.

That’s probably why OpenAI at DevDay made a lot of remarks about privacy and the importance of that, especially if they’re trying to court enterprise users with their AI agents. Right now these companies, especially Meta, are trying to flood the market and create a mass market appeal for this stuff. Similar to how ChatGPT became the default AI chatbot, Meta wants to be that for AI agents, and they feel very hungry about it. They want to create a ChatGPT moment for this technology by making Muse the default for the general public.

There’s something really interesting about the idea that a less-than-frontier model wrapped in a better product is actually going to be the success story here versus a bleeding-edge frontier model that is a little bit harder to use.
There’s some dynamic in there that is the history of all consumer tech products, right? The worst product that’s easier to use often wins, but we haven’t seen that yet in AI.

Right. That’s really important to note here because not everyone needs the bleeding-edge frontier model. Software engineers do. They see a huge difference with coding prowess from one model to another, and that’s why they’re always switching. But the general public, if they’re using an AI agent, as long as it’s useful, they’re good.

However, not many of them are useful yet. We’re still testing Muse and Dots ourselves. For Muse, I saw a couple anecdotes yesterday that it had a big flop for a day or so. People felt like the capabilities got a lot worse. For Dots, the jury’s still out. We’re still testing it.

It depends on what industry you’re in and what you’re really using this stuff for. That’s why OpenAI is going for enterprise, because it makes money and they’re confident that their agent is going to be more and more helpful in these niche industries.

That’s also why they launched specialist Dots, because as we know, the more specialized, niche info you feed into an agent or model, the better it’s going to perform. They don’t want to have that imbued into every single general-purpose agent. It’s just too pricey and too compute heavy, so they say, “You know what? Let’s launch these specialists.”

I feel like you and I talk about consumer versus enterprise adoption of AI every time you’re on this show, and here it seems very important to note that OpenAI asking people to pay a lot of money and asking people to use it primarily in enterprise context is gonna overcome what I think of as the brittleness problem, just because enterprise and business customers have a lot of economic incentives to figure out how to make something work.

If I’m paying OpenAI $100 a month, and I’m using the marketing Dot to solve some marketing automation, and it doesn’t work the first time, it is very likely I will try again. Because if I get it right, then maybe I’ve saved some money or some time in my business that is really good, and I’ll do it again, and eventually that will lead to more revenue for me, the business owner. What I know about consumers is that the first time it doesn’t work, they just walk away. They have no incentive to try again to overcome frustration or brokenness.

We’ve seen this happen with Muse now a few times. I’ve seen it myself with Muse, where it pops open a browser and tries to do something, and it runs into a brick wall or a CAPTCHA or Amazon blocking it, and it says, “I can’t do it that way. Do you want me to try another way?” And I say, “Whatever. I was just screwing around, and I’m never gonna try it again.”

163a6f2d95867fe6: ArtCraft has added alternatives to Microsoft Word, Excel, and PowerPoint to its growing collection of Rust applications, which it describes as "clean-room reimplementations" of proprietary software. That said, "the legal situation is always going to be interesting, and quite possibly litigated, when the party most likely to feel aggrieved has deep pockets and lots of lawyers, and probably quite a lot to lose." ArtCraft says WordCraft was built from public specifications and observation, using original or openly licensed assets. d93f265d1b113a9e: BEIJING: Millions of gig workers in China could benefit from stronger labour protections under proposed rules announced Thursday that would mandate online platforms sign employment contracts with them.

The draft measures from China's human resources and social security ministry require internet platforms that "recruit, organise, and manage workers... to complete platform work tasks" to enter into standardised employment agreements with their workers.
The draft, open for public consultation until Nov 8, could affect millions of takeout delivery drivers, parcel couriers and ride-hailing drivers who often lack formal labour contracts.

Online platforms, including tech giants like Alibaba, Meituan and DiDi, will also be forbidden from encouraging gig workers to register as individual business owners to avoid signing employment contracts with them.
Currently, many gig workers in China are employed as freelancers or through subcontractors.
The world's second-largest economy had 280 million flexible workers in 2025, according to a report by the China New Employment Forms Research Centre, a think tank.
They have few protections and face long working hours for relatively low pay in sectors like food delivery that are characterised by fierce competition and price wars between rival online platforms.
Under the new rules, gig workers will be entitled to the minimum wage, extra pay for work on public holidays, and "appropriate rest".

Platforms must also explain their management algorithms to workers, according to the proposal, and decisions to stop orders or ban worker accounts cannot be made by algorithm alone and must be reviewed manually.

In April, Chinese authorities said they would strengthen management of the gig economy through better legal protections for workers, targeting "substantial progress" in working conditions within three years.

2c54cfec9c5b7bf0: SINGAPORE: Formula One will use the same power unit software fix hurriedly introduced in Malaysia last Sunday if this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix turns wet, the sport's governing body, the International Automobile Federation (FIA), said on Thursday.

The FIA carried out an investigation after what it described as a software bug caused chaos, with cars slowing to a crawl on two formation laps held after heavy rain at Sepang had forced the start of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to be aborted.
The Bahrain Grand Prix was held in Malaysia due to the Iran war and the situation in the Middle East.

The review concluded that some cars running on low engine revs at certain points of the circuit experienced a "loss of power beyond the original intent and that could not be recovered in those sectors.
"As a result, the configuration established for the Sepang event will be reinstated for the Singapore Grand Prix should similar weather conditions be expected.
"Additionally, a further update to the wet weather software will be released for the US Grand Prix on Oct 25," it stated.
Singapore is hosting a sprint race for the first time on Saturday with the main grand prix at night under floodlights on Sunday.

A heat hazard has already been declared by the FIA for the weekend at the Marina Bay circuit, meaning temperatures in excess of 31℃ are forecast, requiring teams to fit a driver cooling system, such as a liquid-cooled vest, though they are not obliged to use them and can take a ballast penalty instead.
The review also recommended implementing measures for testing of the software to make it as robust as possible and the FIA said it would be working with teams and manufacturers.

FIA single-seater director Nikolas Tombazis told reporters on Sunday that the lack of pre-season testing in wet conditions, with Sepang the first wet start of the season, played a part in the chaos but the governing body clarified that.

"Before implementation, teams and power unit manufacturers conducted simulation exercises to validate the software package, which was subsequently tested in full-scale running during Free Practice One sessions at both the Belgian Grand Prix and the Dutch Grand Prix," it said.
Issue identified within five minutes
The FIA also published a chronology of events at Sepang, with the start procedure suspended at 3.45pm local time and the cause of the issue identified within five minutes.
It said teams were given technical guidance and clarification at 4.03pm about installing and operating the revised software configurations.
The integration process was completed by 4.20pm and cars left the pit lane again at 4.33pm.
Red Bull's Max Verstappen, who won in Sepang, said he hoped the next set of regulations would simplify matters, allowing him to jump in the car and "just drive off" instead of waiting for updates.
"The problem is that, as you can see, there is all the software in the background that can make you not pull away or there is a glitch, or even on slow laps, stuff that can happen," he said.
"You shouldn't be thinking about where to be having to lift off or going down a gear to make sure that you have better deployment, all these kinds of things.
"That's not what racing should be about. You should be able to go out, have a brake pedal and a throttle pedal, and that's what decides the lap time," he added.
Drivers are expected to discuss the situation with the FIA at the Singapore race.
"It's something that we need to learn from and make sure it doesn't happen again," said Cadillac's Mexican driver Sergio Perez.

7c196c46d8409f9d: MATAKING, Oct 8 — The palm-sized green turtle hatchling flailing through the sand on a Malaysian island may seem vulnerable, but its species has emerged as a symbol of hope for wildlife conservation.
Green turtles have made the rare jump from endangered to “least concern” in global conservation rankings, a remarkable success when many species are declining.
Conservation NGO World Wildlife Fund (WWF), in its biannual Living Planet Report released Thursday, found a 73-per cent decline in the average size of monitored wildlife populations over 53 years.
But around 50 per cent of the thousands of vertebrates monitored for the report are stable or increasing.
That includes green turtles, thanks to decades of efforts including egg relocation, marine protection and trade bans.
Malaysian turtle expert Juanita Joseph has spent years on the frontlines, carrying out cutting-edge genetic research and even convincing her own father to stop eating turtle eggs.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The palm-size green turtle hatchling flailing its flippers through the sand towards the sea on Mataking Island. — AFP pic
Still, when the International Union for the Conservation of Nature last year announced green turtles were no longer endangered, she could hardly believe it.
“Never in my mind (did I think) that one day turtles can be ‘least concern’. I cried... I said I’ve done my part,” she told AFP at Universiti Malaysia Sabah, where she is a professor.
All six other sea turtle species are still vulnerable or critically endangered, apart from the flatback turtle, whose status is unclear because of data shortages.
Turtles are targeted for food and their shells, killed in fishing nets, and constrained by development and pollution at nesting beaches and feeding grounds.
Climate change also skews populations more female because heat determines sex development in eggs.
Even now, recovery is uneven. While green turtles globally are “least concern”, some regional populations are still endangered and declining.
‘Our heritage’
Malaysia is something of a regional exception. Green turtle nesting at Sabah state’s Turtle Islands has tripled since the 1970s to over 20,000 nests annually.
That reflects “over five decades” of work, said Sabah Parks director Maklarin Lakim.
The Turtle Islands have been protected since 1977, and Sabah banned turtle meat and egg consumption in 1997.
“This is our heritage, this is our biodiversity,” Maklarin said.
“We would like to protect that as long as possible.”
Much of the conservation success has relied on people like Sitti Rasah Abdul, 50, from a fishing community on Malaysia’s Omadal island.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A conservationist counting hatched sea turtles from broken eggshells inside a sandy nesting enclosure. — AFP pic
Since 2012, she and other members of a women’s cooperative have relocated turtle eggs from beaches to a hatchery to protect them from predators and poachers.
The 20-strong team started conservation work with WWF, but now self-funds, ploughing 10 per cent of revenue from their handicraft and catering business into turtle protection.
“I’m already old,” said Rasah, on the wooden jetty that extends from her home into aquamarine seawater.
“But I feel a sense of responsibility to ensure that there are still turtles around for the next generation.”
A 45-minute boat ride away, green and hawksbill turtle hatchlings emerged from relocated nests in a hatchery at the high-end Mataking Reef Resort.
Hotel owner Sophia Sie fell in love with turtles decades ago when her father acquired land on Mataking island, and now around 10 per cent of her staff works on conservation.
In 2006, “we had about 600 eggs collected... today we have about 36,000 eggs,” Sie told AFP.
Guests can release hatchlings, and while Sie considers conservation a passion, it is also good business.
“The survival of our business here is very much dependent on the natural resources and the beauty around us,” she said.
‘Long-term project’
The hatchlings tipped from a basket onto a Mataking beach face long odds. Just one in 1,000 will survive to sexual maturity at 20 years old.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
An adult green sea turtle gliding through the deep blue waters off the coast of Mataking Island. — AFP pic
Hatchlings spend around a decade in the open ocean, a period sometimes called the “lost years” because scientists know so little about it.
Working out where turtles spend those years, and where they forage and reproduce, is key to sustaining conservation success, said Gavin Jolis, marine species strategy manager at WWF-Malaysia.
The NGO has created the world’s first global turtle DNA database, Shellbank, using samples from turtle tissue and shells to trace populations and even target poachers.
“In order to save sea turtles, we have to look at the life cycle,” said Jolis.
“That’s where the genetic work comes in.”
The neat rows of test tubes in Joseph’s lab contain bits of hatchling flipper snipped from babies that did not survive.
Sequencing them reveals a turtle’s “haplotype”, a kind of genetic fingerprint.
The work has already helped show that turtles foraging in parts of Malaysia come from Micronesia, and identified the likely source of turtle shell intercepted in Britain.
While each conservation effort faces different challenges, the battle to protect green turtles teaches “to really be resilient and patient with the work”, said Jolis.
“We should not look at just a short-term project, it’s a long-term project.” — AFP
dc295c84f4c7eb30: DUNGUN, Oct 8 — The surviving rows of two-storey wooden shophouses, known locally as ‘kedai kayu’, in Kuala Dungun are more than remnants of traditional architecture; they stand as witnesses to the history of a town once the centre of trade and economic activity in the district.
Built in 1933, the wooden buildings still carry the character of a bygone era, with timber main structures and windows, though some have been modified over the years to meet modern business needs.
Kuala Dungun trader and resident Ang Ah Kiang, 76, said the buildings are closely linked to the town’s history, which saw it develop from a fishing village into an important trading centre.

He said Kuala Dungun’s role later changed as economic activity picked up following the rapid development of the iron ore mining industry in Bukit Besi, particularly from the 1930s to the 1960s, before the mine closed in 1970.
“The economic growth also indirectly spurred trade in Kuala Dungun, including the emergence of various shops supplying the needs of residents and workers,” he told Bernama when met here today.
The surviving rows of two-storey wooden shophouses in Kuala Dungun. — Bernama pic

Ang said the wooden shops still operating today show the continuity between Kuala Dungun’s trading activities in the past and its business activities today, noting that some of the wooden shops in Kuala Dungun were built between 1930 and 1960.

He said about 100 wooden shop units were built during the period, and the premises now house a range of businesses, including restaurants, hardware stores, electrical shops, motorcycle dealers, plastic goods shops, grocery stores and photo shops.
Meanwhile, restaurant operator Mohd Kamal Hamid, 59, said he has rented the more than 90-year-old shop since 1986, after his father rented the premises in 1980.
He said that although the wooden shop, which he rents for RM1,200 a month, has undergone several renovations, its original structure has been preserved.
“I was told that the original owner of this wooden shop was a former employee of the iron ore mining company in Bukit Besi, and that the building was purchased in the 1930s,” he said.
Mural magic captures everyday life at Kuala Dungun’s ‘kedai kayu’. — Bernama pic

Meanwhile, the Dungun chapter of the Malaysian Historical Society honorary secretary Wan Mohd Rosli Wan Ngah said that in 1933, the Dungun District Office reorganised Kuala Dungun by creating wooden shop lots as a commercial centre to support the growth of trade in the area.
According to him, more Chinese residents were settling in Kuala Dungun at the time, purchasing land and newly completed wooden shophouses.
“Malay residents living in Kuala Dungun were relocated to a new and more comfortable village, Kampung Tanah Lot,” he said.
However, he said Hokkien Chinese from southern China had begun migrating to the district as early as 1922, with many settling along the outskirts of the Sungai Dungun estuary.
“They came to open businesses such as grocery, seafood and rubber shops, and later dominated the wooden shophouses in Kuala Dungun after the town was reorganised in 1933,” he added. — Bernama
e8c1b9c359d7d7ab: MOSCOW, Oct 8 — The death of a plague laboratory worker in Siberia last week has made global headlines, with Russian media suggesting hundreds were under quarantine and US President Donald Trump expressing concern.

Russia has attributed the worker’s death to pneumonia of an “undetermined” cause, but the United States, European Union and World Health Organization (WHO) have all called for more information on the case.
Russia’s public health agency, Rospotrebnadzor, said Wednesday that there was no risk of an epidemic among the wider public.
Here is what we know, five days since the laboratory worker died:
What happened?
The incident was first reported in local media on Friday.

Russian news outlet People of Baikal said that an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute, whom it named as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, died the previous night from a suspected case of pneumonic plague.
She may have contracted the disease from a broken test tube, the outlet reported, without elaborating.
Alexei Tsydenov, governor of the neighbouring Buryatia region, said in a social media post that a woman in the Irkutsk region had “died of plague”, before editing the post to add the word “possibly”.
AFP has not been able to verify the reports.
The mayor of the town of Shelekhov, where she was reported to have died, said a local hospital had been quarantined.
As many as 200 people with whom she may have had contact were placed under quarantine over the incident, People of Baikal said.
Irkutsk is a remote Siberian city home to around 500,000 people in eastern Russia, while Shelekhov is a satellite town to the city’s west.
How has Russia responded?
Russian officials have downplayed or rejected reports the worker died of plague.
The Irkutsk region governor, Igor Kobzev, said Monday that an inspection by Rospotrebnadzor found she died of pneumonia of “undetermined” origin.

“No micro-organisms linked to the young woman’s professional work were found in her biological samples,” Kobzev said, adding that no other staff at the institute had sought medical attention since her death.
Rospotrebnadzor said Wednesday that the situation in the Irkutsk region remained “stable”, and that nearly 5,000 tests had been conducted, none of which revealed dangerous pathogens.
It also reported “comprehensive preventive and anti-epidemic measures” had been implemented, without saying what the measures were.
What is plague?
Plague is a disease caused by the Yersinia pestis bacterium, the same pathogen that killed millions of people in Europe during the Middle Ages.
It can occur in several forms, among them pneumonic plague, which is the most contagious type and can be transmitted by respiratory means. Bubonic plague is transmitted by infected fleas.
All forms can be treated with antibiotics, although can be rapidly fatal if not treated early.
Plague is found in all continents except Oceania, and cases have been sporadically reported worldwide.
A plague outbreak on the island nation of Madagascar killed over 200 people in 2017.
How has the world reacted?
The Russian reports have triggered international concern, with Trump saying Monday that Washington was closely following events.
The WHO, European Union and United States have all called for Russia to be more transparent about the incident.

“WHO has requested further information to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia,” WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said Wednesday, mentioning “media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause”.
Trump said Monday that Washington would “help” Russia, without elaborating. The next day he said he would call Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to discuss the reports.
What is the risk?
Russia has played down the risk.
Rospotrebnadzor said Wednesday that there were no “epidemic risks to the populations of Irkutsk and the Irkutsk Region”.
The WHO initially deemed the risk for the region to be “moderate to low”, but later said it lacked information to conduct a “full risk assessment”.
The Kremlin has hit out at reports of a suspected second case of the disease, saying most of what the media was reporting was “false information”.
Public health experts have also called for calm over the incident, which comes several years after the Covid pandemic.

In previous plague outbreaks, health authorities have had to “find the affected people, find their contacts, quarantine them and give them antibiotics,” Simon Clarke — an associate professor in cellular microbiology at the University of Reading in Britain — told Times Radio on Tuesday.
“It requires a lot of resources. But the Russians should be able to manage this,” he said. — AFP
6930d9caaa3c1f5d: GENEVA, Oct 8 — El Nino will intensify even more before peaking in December, the United Nations said Thursday, warning it could be among the strongest witnessed since at least 1950.

The naturally occurring weather phenomenon is set to bring higher temperatures to much of the planet, the UN’s weather and climate agency said, with its impact compounding the effects of man-made climate change.
“El Nino will continue to intensify ahead of its forecast peak in December,” the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said in its monthly Global Seasonal Climate Update.
“It is likely to bring above-average temperatures to much of the globe and shift rainfall patterns, increasing the risk of drought and floods in different regions.”
El Nino warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns.
It typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months.
Conditions oscillate between El Nino and its opposite La Nina, with neutral conditions in between.
El Nino ‘strengthening rapidly’

“Sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific are forecast to increase to record levels during October-November-December 2026, reflecting the strengthening of the El Nino event which will drive weather patterns and impact economies, ecosystems and communities across the globe,” the WMO said.
The forecast is based on consensus across 13 leading national and international meteorological centres.
“El Nino is firmly established and strengthening rapidly,” said WMO chief Celeste Saulo.
“WMO forecasts indicate a near-100 percent likelihood that it will persist through February 2027, potentially being one of the strongest since at least 1950.”
Saulo explained that El Nino does not add new heat to the planet, but releases heat being stored in the ocean.
“The ocean it’s drawing from is the warmest we’ve ever measured it. There is simply more heat available to release,” she said.
Sea temperatures record

The index which measures sea surface temperature anomalies across the central-eastern equatorial Pacific — the region at the heart of El Nino — increased from 1.6C above normal in June to 2.5C above normal in August.
For October-November-December, the anomaly is forecast to reach approximately 3.7C above normal.
This would be the highest since observations began, eclipsing the previous record of 2.6C set in 2015-2016.
The last El Nino contributed to making 2023 the second-hottest year on record and 2024 the all-time high at around 1.55C above the 1850-1900 pre-industrial average.
While El Nino usually peaks between November and February, the resulting spike in temperatures typically comes later.
This El Nino is already hitting some regions hard, including in Central America, where animals and crops are dying from drought. — AFP

23e939f5f82ff409: KUALA LUMPUR: Parlimen bukan tempat sesuai untuk perbincangan mengenai reformasi nasional yang kontroversi kerana ahli politik sering terikat dengan pendirian parti dan pertimbangan pilihan raya, kata Nazir Razak.

Pengerusi Yayasan Tun Razak itu berkata, Ahli Parlimen cenderung mematuhi arahan whip parti dan menjaga sokongan penyokong masing-masing, menyebabkan mereka sukar menyuarakan pandangan secara bebas mengenai isu sensitif.

“Di Parlimen, ahli politik perlu menjaga sokongan penyokong masing-masing dan pada masa sama mengikut arahan whip parti. Jadi, respons atau hujah dikemukakan sering dipengaruhi faktor lain, bukan semata-mata berdasarkan pandangan mereka sendiri tentang apa yang terbaik atau pandangan sebenar mereka terhadap sesuatu masalah.
“Sebab itu, sesetengah reformasi struktur sistem yang paling berjaya dibincangkan di luar Parlimen terlebih dahulu sebelum dibawa ke Parlimen,” katanya.
Beliau berkata demikian pada Dialog Seri Negara 2026 yang dirasmikan Menteri Perpaduan Negara Aaron Ago Dagang.

Nazir mengulangi gesaannya supaya Majlis Perundingan Negara kedua diwujudkan sebagai platform membincangkan isu termasuk tindakan afirmatif, identiti nasional, keseimbangan kuasa institusi dan rasuah.

Bekas Pengerusi Kumpulan CIMB itu menjadikan proses perbincangan Ireland mengenai reformasi undang-undang pengguguran sebagai contoh bagaimana isu sukar boleh dibincangkan terlebih dahulu di luar Parlimen sebelum cadangan dikemukakan kepada penggubal undang-undang.

Bagaimanapun, Ahli Parlimen Bangi, Syahredzan Johan, berkata ahli politik perlu dilibatkan kerana mereka sering menjadi pihak pertama menerima aduan rakyat dan memahami masalah dihadapi penduduk di kawasan masing-masing.
Katanya, media sosial juga memberikan gambaran mengelirukan mengenai Parlimen apabila pergeseran antara mereka lebih mendapat perhatian berbanding perbincangan mengenai dasar.

Syahredzan memberi contoh Jawatankuasa Pilihan Khas Parlimen yang membolehkan Ahli Parlimen daripada parti berbeza bekerjasama secara konstruktif apabila perbincangan dilakukan tanpa liputan atau tekanan untuk mendapatkan perhatian umum.

Beliau bersetuju perbincangan tanpa liputan mungkin lebih produktif, namun berkata ahli politik tetap perlu mengambil bahagian bersama wakil sektor lain dengan kepentingan nasional mengatasi kepentingan politik.

Ketua Pegawai Eksekutif Institut Demokrasi dan Hal Ehwal Ekonomi (IDEAS), Aira Azhari, mencadangkan sistem pilihan raya first-past-the-post Malaysia dikaji semula kerana sistem sedia ada mungkin menyumbang kepada politik yang semakin berpecah-belah.
Beliau berkata, perubahan komposisi etnik Malaysia, termasuk penyusutan jumlah penduduk bukan Melayu, boleh mempengaruhi politik pilihan raya serta cara parti politik bersaing mendapatkan sokongan.

Aira turut memberi amaran persepsi mengenai saiz ekonomi yang semakin mengecil boleh meningkatkan persaingan antara komuniti apabila setiap kelompok melihat keuntungan pihak lain sebagai kerugian kepada mereka.

Katanya, sistem pilihan raya first-past-the-post, apabila digabungkan dengan perpecahan sedia ada dalam masyarakat, boleh menyumbang kepada persaingan politik yang berasaskan pendekatan menang-kalah, iaitu keuntungan satu pihak dilihat sebagai kerugian pihak lain.

“Ada sesuatu dalam sistem itu sendiri yang boleh diubah suai dan mungkin mengubah cara permainan politik berlangsung,” katanya, namun tidak menghuraikan perubahan perlu dibuat terhadap sistem pilihan raya itu.
58eb7bfbae6cd914: PETALING JAYA: Transport minister Loke Siew Fook has denied that the Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link is delayed, following the announcement that operations would begin in mid-February 2027.
Loke said the project's physical construction remained on schedule for completion on Dec 31, while additional time was needed simply to conduct comprehensive safety assessments and system tests.
While operations could technically begin in January, both countries agreed to allow more time to ensure the service operates safely and smoothly, Berita Harian reported.
"It is not delayed. The project's physical construction will be completed on Dec 31.

"We agreed that the best decision is to start the service in February 2027 to ensure that all safety measures are properly implemented. We do not want to take the risk of rushing the opening," he was quoted as saying.
Loke added that the stations as well as customs, immigration and quarantine complexes in both countries had also been completed.
He said October to December would be used to test the integration of key systems, including signalling, passenger management, train operations and cross-border coordination.
The minister said the exact opening date would be announced once final approval is obtained from the transport authorities of both countries.

The RTS Link will connect Bukit Chagar in Johor Bahru with Woodlands North in Singapore. It is designed with a peak capacity of up to 10,000 passengers per hour in each direction, with the journey between the two stations expected to take about five minutes.
95b92ac642cfc5bb: BANGKOK: Thai authorities began extradition proceedings on Thursday against a Chinese investigative reporter wanted by Beijing and detained for months in Thailand, his lawyer and an official told AFP.
Bai Zhaodong, 56, exposed government corruption in China over two decades before leaving in 2023 to escape "mounting persecution from the state", according to Reporters Without Borders (RSF).
Bai, who is recognised by the UN as a refugee, arrived in Thailand in 2024 and has been detained in the Southeast Asian country since January 2026, the media rights group says.
Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian said in July that Bai was suspected of extortion and bribery, and an extradition request had been submitted to Thailand.

"The prosecutor is bringing a case against him at court now. It is the beginning of the extradition hearing process," Prayuth Pecharakun, spokesman for Thailand's attorney general, told AFP on Thursday.
He said the process could take months.
Bai's lawyer Nadthasiri Bergman also confirmed to AFP that he had been taken to court to face extradition proceedings.
The hearing had not previously been made public, and RSF advocacy manager Aleksandra Bielakowska called the development "scandalous".
It came the day before an expected decision on a legal challenge brought by Bai's lawyers against Thai authorities over his continued detention.

"Bringing Bai Zhaodong before a court without notice, on the eve of a decision on the legality of his detention, is scandalous and shows how eager the Thai authorities are to bow to Beijing's demands," Bielakowska said.
RSF believes his life could be at risk if he is returned to China.
"We call on the international community to demand that Bangkok halt his deportation and allow him to travel safely to the country of his choice," Bielakowska said.

f284485ad4de458b: Ten of the world's biggest AI developers have agreed to tighten their handling of personal data following scrutiny by Britain's privacy watchdog, which is now turning its attention to autonomous AI agents that don't always play by the rules. The recently rebranded Information Commission's Office (ICO) said Thursday that Amazon, Anthropic, Apple, Cohere, DeepSeek, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Stability AI have either made changes or committed to doing so after the regulator examined their compliance with UK data protection law. These include clearer explanations of how personal information is used to train AI models, better ways for people to exercise their data rights, and tougher assessments of developers' safeguards. The commitments follow a supervisory program launched in 2025 that initially covered 11 developers. That number dropped to ten after the ICO paused its engagement with Elon Musk's xAI to pursue a separate formal investigation into its Grok chatbot. The watchdog isn't declaring victory just yet. It's monitoring whether developers deliver on their promises and admits that current AI training practices still pose problems under UK data protection law. Developers still have some explaining to do over personal data buried in their models, particularly sensitive information, and how people are supposed to get their details removed once an AI has been trained on them. There's also the risk of personal information being extracted from models, including data developers never intended them to retain. The ICO acknowledged that some of these issues will require cooperation between industry, regulators, and government. Getting companies to promise changes is one thing. Making today's AI models comply with the law is another. "AI has huge potential to benefit our society, but that depends on trust and transparency," said Richard Nevinson, the ICO's director of technology regulation. "Our engagement with some of the biggest developers has secured real commitments that will help people better understand and control how their data is used, even in a fast-moving and complex area." Meanwhile, the regulator is turning its attention to AI agents, which can browse websites, use tools, and carry out tasks with limited human supervision. And some aren't sticking to the rules. The ICO confirmed it has contacted OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and the UK's AI Security Institute following reports of agents bypassing safeguards during testing and deployment earlier this year. "These recent reports show both how fast these systems are advancing, and the risks they pose if the guardrails aren't fit for purpose," Nevinson said. "Our message is clear: the fact AI agents act with autonomy is not an excuse for poor compliance." The regulator has also launched a six-week call for evidence on agentic AI, covering security, transparency, accountability, and the lawful use of personal data. Responses are due by November 20 and will inform future guidance and the ICO's forthcoming statutory code of practice on AI and automated decision-making. The watchdog is separately examining how consumer chatbots and AI companions use personal information as they become increasingly personalized. For now, the ICO has secured promises from some of the industry's biggest names, although whether they deliver remains to be seen. And with AI agents increasingly capable of acting on their own, the watchdog may have its work cut out keeping them in line. ®

eb83ef4fd58a7c7d: KUALA LUMPUR: Yayasan Tun Razak chairman Nazir Razak says Parliament is not the appropriate place for initial discussions on contentious national reforms as politicians are often constrained by party positions and electoral considerations.
Nazir said politicians were expected to follow party whips and appeal to their supporters, making it difficult for them to express their views freely on sensitive issues.

“In Parliament, politicians have to play to their gallery and act according to their whip. So the responses or the arguments are often dictated by other forces rather than what, in their own opinion, is the best view or the honest view of a particular problem.

“That's why some of the most successful structural reforms of systems have been done offline and then taken to Parliament,” he said during the Seri Negara Dialogue 2026 here today, which was officiated by national unity minister Aaron Ago Dagang.

Nazir reiterated his call for a second National Consultative Council to provide a platform for discussions on issues such as affirmative action, national identity, the balance of institutional powers and corruption.

The former CIMB Group chairman cited Ireland's deliberative process on abortion reform as an example of how difficult issues could first be discussed outside Parliament before proposals were brought to lawmakers.

Bangi MP Syahredzan Johan said politicians must be involved in such discussions as they were often the first to receive complaints from ordinary Malaysians and understood the problems affecting their constituents.
He said social media also gave a misleading impression of Parliament, with confrontations between MPs gaining more traction than substantive policy discussions.
Syahredzan cited parliamentary select committees as examples of how MPs from opposing parties could work constructively when discussions took place without cameras or pressure to play to the gallery.

He agreed that discussions without cameras could be more productive, but said politicians should participate alongside representatives from other sectors, with national interests taking precedence over political interests.

Institute for Democracy and Economic Affairs CEO Aira Azhari suggested reviewing Malaysia's first-past-the-post electoral system, saying the current system could be contributing to increasingly divisive politics.
She said Malaysia's changing ethnic composition, including a shrinking non-Malay population, would affect electoral politics and how political parties compete for support.
Aira also warned that the perception of a shrinking economic pie could worsen competition between communities, with each seeing the other's gains as coming at its own expense.
She said the first-past-the-post system, when combined with existing divisions in society, could contribute to this zero-sum political game.

“There is something within the system itself that can be tweaked that might change the rules of the game,” she said. Aira, however, did not elaborate on what changes should be made to the electoral system.
64c66745bf83e2ab: ROME: Italy's parliament on Thursday approved a reform of the country's electoral law that opposition parties say prime minister Giorgia Meloni's hard-right government has designed to boost its chances of re-election next year.
The reform introduces a fully proportional system that guarantees a parliamentary majority to any alliance winning more than 42% of the vote.
Meloni, who has presided over the longest-serving government in Italy's post-war history, has argued the reform will bring more political stability.
The vote passed with 227 votes in favour and 164 against after Meloni told her governing coalition she would resign if the reform fell through.
"Stable governments and greater participation mean more continuity, more accountability and a greater ability to provide concrete answers to Italians," Meloni wrote on X after the vote.
The changes also require parties and coalitions to spell out their governing programme and name their candidate for premier ahead of elections.
Giovanni Donzelli, a senior lawmaker with Meloni's Brothers of Italy party, told AFP the electoral law "is a revolution".
"Italians will finally have real weight with their vote, as they will choose the coalition, the platform, and the candidate for prime minister," he said.

However, Giuseppe Conte, former prime minister and leader of the opposition Five Stars Movement (M5S), told AFP the new law is "a mess, a convoluted scheme, devised solely to find a formula to gain an advantage in the upcoming elections".
Neither the right nor the left are expected to secure an outright parliamentary majority at the next election, which has to be held by the end of next year.
Under the proposed system, an alliance winning more than 42% of the vote would automatically receive a parliamentary majority, gaining an additional 70 seats in the lower house and 35 in the Senate.
Reaching that threshold, however, may prove difficult for either side.

Meloni last month became the leader of the longest-running administration in Italy's postwar history, but her coalition has been losing support to former army general Roberto Vannacci and his new National Future (FN) party.

Although Meloni has so far ruled out an alliance with Vannacci, the far-right FN is polling ahead of both Meloni's allies, the anti-immigrant League and centre-right Forza Italia, and she may yet need him.
According to a recent survey by Ipsos Doxa, the centre-left coalition could surpass the 42% threshold, provided it overcomes internal divisions and persuades two small radical parties to join forces.
Meloni's term officially ends in October 2027, but she could opt to bring elections forward to April or May.
Opposition parties have already vowed to challenge the new electoral law in court before then.

11289be61303f303: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 8 — Schools and educational institutions under the Education Ministry in areas where the Air Pollutant Index (API) exceeds 180 must close from tomorrow (October 9), as authorities step up measures to protect students and teachers from the worsening haze.

“Areas recording API readings above 150 continuously for three consecutive days must close from Monday, October 12, 2026.”
Affected schools must switch to home-based teaching and learning (PdPR) to ensure lessons continue during the closures.
“Schools and educational institutions under the ministry that are affected are required to conduct home-based teaching and learning sessions,” Mohd Azam said.
He added that schools must ensure lessons continue through appropriate methods that take into account students’ capabilities, access and needs, as well as teachers’ preparedness.
Teachers and support staff will also be permitted to work from home during the closures, the ministry said.

State Education Departments, district education offices and educational institutions have been instructed to monitor air quality continuously and take appropriate action when pollution levels exceed the stipulated thresholds.

The latest directive comes as haze continues to affect air quality in parts of Malaysia, raising concerns over prolonged exposure to pollutants, particularly among children and other vulnerable groups.
Under Malaysia’s API classification, readings of 101 to 200 are considered unhealthy, while those between 201 and 300 are classified as very unhealthy.
The directive does not amount to a nationwide school shutdown, with closures determined by air quality readings in the affected areas.

AI breakthroughs in robotics won’t change your life any time soon

The hype around humanoid robots is reaching fever pitch. Much of it comes from the idea that the same AI advances behind ChatGPT and Claude could enable robots to imitate human movement the way chatbots imitate human language. But many researchers are skeptical.

The fighting in Yemen has in recent weeks become the most active front of the wider regional conflict, which for months has seen violence repeatedly shift focus across the Middle East.
In Yemen, one of the world’s poorest countries, it is ordinary civilians paying the price, with more than 200,000 people displaced since July, according to UN data.
After declaring a counter-offensive against the Houthis, Yemen’s government claimed to have pushed the fighters out of strategic areas on the Red Sea and the port city of Mocha.

In Saudi Arabia, the latest blasts came a day after the Houthis claimed attacks on two international airports, while repeating a warning to airlines to avoid Saudi airspace.
Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority said the airports in Riyadh and Abha were “subjected to attacks” on Tuesday and Wednesday.
An Egyptian and an Algerian national were killed at Abha airport, while a Sudanese national was killed at Riyadh airport, the agency said.
The attacks wounded 36 people, it added.
In a subsequent statement, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis blamed them for the strikes and vowed that they “will not go unpunished”.
Humanitarian crisis
Yesterday in Yemen, clashes left at least 62 combatants dead, including 37 Houthis, military sources from both camps told AFP.
Saba also reported that a Houthi missile wounded five civilians in Taiz, a city held by government forces.
“We went out into the street to check on the wounded and saw young civilians who had been hit,” resident Al-Fateh al-Eisaei told AFP.
“The Houthi shell landed in the middle of the street, right in an area crowded with civilians.”
The humanitarian crisis caused by the war has left most of the nation’s population dependent on aid. — AFP
