Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace.

Industrial AI may not be new, but it is developing at a breakneck pace. From modern predictive analytics that can preempt equipment failures, to autonomous robots tasked with inspecting high risk machinery, emerging applications have the potential to transform operational efficiencies. But often used in high consequence environments with minimal margin for error, industrial AI deployed without clarity, security, or accountability could also have catastrophic consequences for critical infrastructure over time. As industries rush to embrace the latest technologies, the goal should always be responsible AI designed to support, rather than replace that all important human judgment.
Two words for you: sustainable automation.
My guest today is Arti Garg, chief technologist at AVEVA.
This podcast is produced in partnership with AVEVA.
Welcome, Arti.
Arti Garg: Thank you, Megan. It’s great to be here.

Megan: Thank you so much for joining us. And just to start, if we could set some context for our discussion, can you share a bit about the current state of industrial AI and what AVEVA is working on at the moment as well?

Arti: Yeah, more than happy to. And I want to go back to what you already stated, which is that in some ways, industrial AI is not new. It’s something that, even here at AVEVA, we’ve been working on for more than 20 years, really thinking about how AI can enhance applications in the industrial sector.

But what has changed quite substantially in maybe the last few years is the type of AI. We’ve really moved to these general purpose foundation models, which enable a lot more people to leverage advanced AI technologies. In addition to that, in just the last couple of years, there’s been an explosion in what’s known as physical AI and the types of AI that can really accelerate the capabilities of robotics and autonomous systems. And also agentic AI, which also allows for automation at more of the software level.

And what we’re seeing is that while in the past there has been some hesitancy to adopt models that don’t totally have predictable outcomes, there’s been a rapid acceleration in adoption of AI even in the industrial sector. One study suggests maybe that’s almost a 78% increase over the past just two years within the industrial sector. So yes, that’s an inflection point, but it’s almost like a step function if you think about it with respect to AI adoption.

And what we’re really thinking about now at AVEVA is, how do we think about this? How do we think about incorporating these new and very powerful AI technologies in environments where customers have mission-critical operations, human safety is a significant factor? Those are some of the primary concerns that our customers have when they think about adopting any new technology. We’re doing that in narrow where these newer types of AI aren’t necessarily predictable, in terms of how they behave. That’s one of the areas we’re really thinking about is, how do we leverage these technologies while maintaining safety, while maintaining reliable operations, while still being able to deliver on the promises of the new capabilities?

Megan: There’s so many things to consider at once, isn’t it? And you outlined there some of the huge developments we’ve seen in this space in recent years. What makes this such a pivotal moment for industrial AI specifically? What has changed to make some of those perhaps more out there hypotheticals much more plausible?

Arti: Well, I think one of the big things, one of the big challenges within industrial AI, and this is something that as AVEVA, it’s in our blood, it’s in our core DNA, is that to really leverage any kind of digital technology in the industrial space, one of the first important things you often need to do is gather and correlate data from disparate systems, so that maybe I have telemetry coming off of a pump or a mixer, and I want to be able to correlate that with service logs so I know maybe the last time that someone had done some maintenance on that pump or mixer. And maybe I also want to be able to correlate that with the original design documentation and some of the original documentation on how to maintain that, so that if something is happening, I can do a better job diagnosing what’s going wrong and how to address it. This has always been a core challenge in the industrial space.

I think that what’s happening now is that with newer technologies, even things like graph databases and being able to leverage AI to really match disparate data sets much faster, we’re able to get to the point where if something goes wrong, instead of an operator maybe needing to spend a little bit of time doing this research to really understand how do these different components fit together of information, they may have just an iPad with an AI that can very quickly go and fetch that information, correlate it and help in real time, almost, diagnose what is happening.

Even a little bit more out there, but not as out there as you might think is, I still describe this with a human operator with potentially a mobile tablet, but imagine now I can also have a robot moving through that environment also gathering data and either with onboard computation or a quick connection to an operator who doesn’t necessarily now have to go out into a dangerous, potentially somewhat hazardous space, be able to gather data and enable that very quick diagnostic as well. And I think that’s really what’s exciting right now and what all of these new technologies that I’ve talked about are helping to enable.

And I think then from our perspective, trying to really leverage all of those means that we have to think a lot now about our governance approach to this. How do we leverage AI in a way that keeps it contained, if you will?
Megan: Yeah, absolutely. And on that governance point, how does AVEVA define responsible AI and what do you see as the primary benefits?

Arti: Yeah, so I think for us, we think about a triple mandate around responsible AI, and that means that it’s secure, it’s efficient, and that includes environmentally efficient, and then it really preserves human safety and human oversight above all. And for us, that’s what some of our core pillars of responsible AI include. And for us, that means we think about internally as we build tools, a multi-layered governance approach where we’ve got both for how we use AI as a company and then how we deploy AI into our products. We’ve got a similar framework that we leverage across both, a kind of joint governance model, both around how we’re leveraging AI and also how we’re infusing AI into our products to allow our customers to leverage AI in their operations.

But I would say one of the core foundational principles underneath all of these is that human beings still remain centered in how we think about how AI is leveraged. And so human judgment, human responsibility, human ethics are still core to how we think about where AI can add benefits, and we think about it more as augmenting rather than replacing human beings in critical decision loops, if you will.

Megan: Right, which is such an important distinction, isn’t it? And in terms of the next phase of development, there’s growing sentiment that agentic AI will soon allow these industrial systems to operate much more autonomously. I wonder, what makes the risks in industrial settings different from AI risk in a purely digital context? And I suppose on the flip side, what are the benefits and opportunities of that same software defined automation?

Arti: I think we can start with the risks and then go to the benefits. I think ultimately, I would say the biggest risk in the industrial setting is that we are interacting with real physical systems, often physical systems that are very capable of delivering important outcomes that keep our world running, whether that’s delivering power, whether that’s mining for natural resources. But usually. Those physical systems are also operating in hazardous environments, the equipment itself is capable of also having human safety implications. Anytime you’re interfacing software with a physical system that can have real world consequences, you have to be extra careful. And we’ve always had that, again, we’ve had that in our DNA at AVEVA from the beginning, being mindful of that end user and that end application, which is not just something on a computer screen.

Even as we’ve deployed AI over the past few decades into our systems, we’ve typically leaned toward really trying to pick the best fit model, really understand that model’s behavior if we’re going to use, for example, we have a proprietary anomaly detection model that works in a lot of operational environments. Now, as we’re thinking about some of these newer AI capabilities, which by design are hard to understand how they behave, they’re not fundamentally explainable in the way we’ve thought about even AI or statistical models in the past, and actually their behavior can change over time as they learn and get tuned to new capabilities. That’s really the potential risk of automating a physical system based on capabilities that can evolve over time is one of the things that we have to be really mindful of and really thoughtful around, where are we willing to put some of that increased automation into practice?

But at the same time, I think there’s a real opportunity there, because I glossed over this idea that, okay, well, models evolve, but so do human beings, and sometimes that’s a good thing. We talk about humans having expertise and they gain understanding over their careers of how a system works. If we can actually leverage the ability of some of these newer AI capabilities, these sort of reasoning models often have underlying agentic capabilities, to learn and gather experience faster, and potentially even more importantly or more valuably, take experience that’s learned at one site and apply it to another site, then that’s a real opportunity to take what we already know works for human beings, which is that sometimes you just have to learn by doing and be able to apply that and scale that through AI. That’s where I see potentially a real opportunity in this space.

One of the things that we’re really aware of in the industrial sector is just the way that our workforce is changing. I think that almost half, not quite half, of the industrial workforce is set to retire in the next five years, and that’s a lot of expertise and experience that means that we’re going to lose in the sector. If there’s ways to make sure that we can capture that in ways that are actionable, in ways that can also help a newer generation of workers that are used to experience things in a different way, apply that expertise, apply that knowledge, then I think that’s a huge opportunity within the industrial space.

Megan: Yeah, absolutely. Clearly, some huge opportunities there particularly against the backdrop of other market and workforce changes as you’ve outlined there. I suppose building on that, what is the potential for these autonomous industrial AI systems when built and deployed responsibly to facilitate even faster, more sustainable industrial processes?

Arti: I think there’s a couple different ways to think about this. One is, what are the demands of potentially more environmentally sustainable processes? I’ll use one example of something that my team has been working on in partnership with Idaho National Laboratory here in the U.S. as part of their testing for AI grid resilience project.

One of the challenges in the electric grid as we’re moving toward a future where we have a lot more intermittent renewable power generation sources, often distributed rooftop solar for example, is it’s becoming much more challenging to manage the grid both from really understanding where electric capacity is coming in, electric load is pulling off of the grid. In addition to that, being able to maintain just power quality because instead of having one spinning asset delivering the frequency of electricity that’s going across the grid, you’ve got a lot of smaller systems. AI is actually quite critical for being able to manage that grid of the future. And this is one of the things that we’ve been working in partnership is, how can we do that? How can we help grid operators better understand what’s happening across their system, identify where things might be behaving anomalously so they can detect that early and then remediate for it?

At the same time though, I always talk about that’s an example of where AI can potentially help us accelerate the transition to a lower carbon energy future. At the same time, I think there’s a lot of conversation around the sustainability of AI itself. What are the power requirements? What are the resource requirements needed to run AI? And before I get into how do we think about that at AVEVA, because it is definitely something we think about and I think a lot of actors in the space are thinking about, I want to point out, is one of the challenges is that there’s really no agreed upon method to measure the environmental impact of AI. You see a lot of these stories, like one query on some kind of chat interface is X amount of gallons of water or this amount of electricity use. But the truth is that community-wide, there’s no agreed upon standard.

One of the things that I’m involved with is a standards working group that was launched by the IEEE two years ago, a little over two years ago. I’m the chair of that working group, it’s called the P7100 Standards Working Group on measuring the environmental impact of AI. And one of the things we’re trying to do is really identify all the different areas over which we want to think about environmental sustainability associated with AI, and then having one standard methodology that works and that can be adopted both from a reporting perspective and potentially also from an oversight or regulatory perspective. That becomes really important for any sort of real understanding of how AI impacts the environment is just we have to know, what does it use? We want to look holistically at that. Our standards cover electricity and energy consumption, it covers resource usage, it covers water consumption, and it also covers carbon.

But all of that said, I think it’s important for us to understand the footprint of AI, but I think it’s also important for us to simultaneously recognize that a bigger model uses more compute and more compute probably leverages more resources. The more that we can be intentional and pick the right size model for the right application, the more we can already start down that path of being more environmentally efficient in the AI that we run. One of the potentially nice side effects of that is the more purpose-built a model, the less likely it is to misbehave in unpredictable ways, if you choose correctly your architecture. There’s some sort of ancillary benefits that go beyond environmental sustainability.

Megan: Fascinating. It’s really, really interesting to hear some of the work going on behind the scenes there, because I think we’ll all have heard some of the statistics around the environmental impact, as you say. So, it’s great to understand some of the work going on there to really clarify that.

And we’ve talked a little bit about AI augmenting humans earlier. As systems gain greater autonomy, how should organizations think about that balance between closed loop automation, human in the loop accountability? What guardrails need to be in place? And how are governments and cross-border actors approaching those concerns as well?

Arti: There’s a lot packed into that question, so I’ll try to answer it somewhat one by one. First, starting with that sort of balance between closed loop and human in the loop, automation and accountability. One of the things that we talk about in the industrial sector is from human operator to human supervisor of systems, of industrial systems. And if I’m honest about that, we’re still trying to figure that out. When a human’s in a loop in an automated system, you’re really thinking about a system may process all the data and then make a recommendation.
9a5d99eb41100f88: Welcome back to PWNED, the weekly column where we highlight some of the lowlights in corporate security. This week, we’ll talk about two scenarios, one that ended in tragedy and another that shows the power of a good defense over dedicated phishing attacks. Have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? Share it with us at pwned@sitpub.com. Anonymity is available upon request. Both stories come courtesy of Dave Hatter, a cybersecurity and compliance consultant with Intrust IT. In his many years of experience with the company, Hatter has had to work for a variety of small companies that needed help with their security, whether they knew it or not. One time several years ago, the new CFO at a small construction company phoned Intrust and expressed interest in hiring them. However, the proposal was vetoed by the owner of the company, an older gentleman who thought his business was too small to interest hackers and that his existing, one-person IT staff was all he could afford. “We got a guy, my brother’s uncle’s cousin does my IT, don’t need you guys,” Hatter quotes the owner as saying. “We hear this all the time. Thanks for shopping. You’re too expensive.” Three weeks later, Hatter got a call from a local accountant friend who begged him to help a client who'd been hit with a ransomware attack. Hatter said he couldn’t really give more than general guidance, but would talk to the victim anyway. As soon as he called the number, Hatter realized that the ransomware victim was actually the same construction company that had turned down his services a few weeks earlier. The business had an old unpatched Windows server that contained all its most important data. There was a backup drive, but it was connected to the same server, so both devices were encrypted by the ransomware. “Their entire backup is this external drive, which, of course, is now encrypted,” Hatter said. “So, literally, they can't pay their employees. They don't know who owes them money.” Hatter could not help the company, and he never found out whether it paid the ransom. However, the org, which had been around for years, went out of business within months. This sad story shows the importance of having real backups that are off-site or in the cloud and patching whatever servers you have. You can never assume that your company is too small to be attacked because ransomware gangs want your money and they are just as happy to take on small businesses as large ones, which are likely to be harder targets. The other incident involved two companies in the landscaping and construction business. Somebody broke into an executive’s email account at company one and started sending phishing emails to company number two. The miscreants had also set up email filtering rules in the first company’s account so that the messages from the phishing campaign were routed to buried folders where the real-life account holder would never see them. The phishing mails took the form of RFPs (requests for proposal) – a perfect lure, because who wouldn't want new business? They were perfectly crafted, with no grammar errors or obvious tells, and the return address matched company one's. However, instead of attaching the RFP as a PDF or PowerPoint file, it had a button for the user to click to download it. “If I can get in your email and send out emails as you, the recipients, especially if they've interacted with me before, aren't going to have any guard up,” Hatter said. “Especially if there's no crazy language or crazy requests in there because they've got an email from me before.” Upon clicking the download button, the user was transported to a Microsoft 365 login screen that looked identical to the real one but was not on the microsoft.com domain. The user was then invited to put in their email address and password to gain access to the desired file. Because the user had 2FA, this fake page also asked them for their limited-time 2FA code. Behind the scenes, the threat actors were transmitting the login to Microsoft so that Microsoft itself would send an SMS message to the victim at company number two. Then the victim would pass along the one-time passcode via the fake login site. A classic man-in-the-middle attack. It worked, and the threat actors now had access to the Microsoft 365 account and email for the victim at company number two. This could've allowed them to do almost anything using that person’s email. If the victim had access to bank accounts or customer data, the attackers could have initiated password resets from the account, then conducted fraudulent money transfers, or stolen personal information. At the very least, they could've used the victim's account to phish other contacts. Fortunately, Hatter's client had installed a piece of software his company made called TarBot, which runs in the Microsoft 365 environment and uses Entra ID P2 to help customers identify suspicious logins. “It throws off a bunch of telemetry, statistics, metrics, whatever you want to call it, that allows our software to say, this is an anomalous login, revoke the token, and make the user log in again,” Hatter said. He said his company is not the only one to make apps like TarBot that detect suspicious logins. So the bad guys were kicked out after just a few minutes. But Hatter says the better way to stop these attacks is to use phishing-resistant MFA, such as hardware keys (like the YubiKey line) or passkeys. With today’s AI-assisted phishing, telltale signs such as bad grammar or obviously fake login pages are becoming few and far between. ®
09103abe493789fb: When implementing any kind of technology, the difference between offering employees training and supporting them in adoption is all too frequently misunderstood. But the difference is a significant one. Training is usually a time-limited, structured educational initiative to help people build technical competence and learn how a system works. Adoption, on the other hand, is a continuous, long-term process by which employees use technology to change how they work in order to deliver more value. Nowhere is this distinction more vital than in the emerging world of agentic AI. To date, many organizations have been experimenting with the technology to automate discrete tasks, particularly in areas such as software engineering, customer support, and operations. Over the next two years though, Gartner expects deployment to jump from the current 17 percent of businesses to more like 60 percent. Their key aims in going down this route include automating complex multistep workflows, boosting operational efficiency, and maximizing productivity. But despite the perceived value of agentic AI here, many organizations are currently struggling to create such value in real terms. This includes generating a return on investment. Identifying the value gap In fact, according to WalkMe's 'The State of Digital Adoption 2026' report, a huge 40 percent of all expenditure on digital transformation underperforms expectations, mainly due to user adoption challenges. As the study, which is based on input from 3,750 respondents worldwide, says: "The technology does what it's supposed to do. The adoption execution around it doesn't." As such, it found the average employee loses a full working day each week (7.9 hours) to "friction". For example, they spend 1.34 hours per week re-entering the same information across multiple applications. Another hour disappears on finding workarounds when tools are unable to communicate effectively. A further 3.69 hours vanish due to a lack of guidance on how to use such tools. This includes 1.03 hours being spent trying to understand unclear instructions. A final 1.88 hours each week are spent on reworking AI prompts and waiting for faulty tools to be fixed. Ofir Hatsor is WalkMe's Senior Vice President of Sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa. He believes that a good chunk of this friction is due to the complex and highly regulated environment in which enterprises function. This means many of them struggle to change how they operate day-to-day - even though it is only in doing so that they can create true value for the business. "There's currently a very big gap between perceived value and existing value, or the actual value that will follow," he points out. "I think over time this gap will be mitigated, but it's not going to be tomorrow - more like the next three, five, or seven years, and in some companies, it'll never close." The difficulties in affecting change As to why affecting meaningful operational change is often so difficult to achieve, especially when moving to an agentic AI environment, Hatsor points to several reasons. The first is a "visibility gap". As WalkMe's study indicates, most executives believe their organizations use an average of 35 applications when the actual number is 661 - a visibility gap of 1,789 percent. For AI-powered tools in particular, leaders estimate teams use 21 when the real count is 80. The point here, as the report says, is that: "You can't optimize workflows you can't see, govern AI tools you don't know exist, or measure productivity when your instrumentation covers a fraction of where work actually happens." A key part of the problem is shadow AI. For instance, 45 percent of workers admitted to using unapproved AI tools in the previous 30 days as authorized systems failed to fit current workflows. Unfortunately, 36 percent of them also used confidential company data in the process. A big challenge, Hatsor explains, is the ease with which employees can get hold of AI development tools today. "So, they create their own little vibe-coding applications and share them between themselves," he says. "But if I'm the chief information officer or chief security officer, my visibility into that landscape is limited at best." This is made even harder when employees aren’t honest with their employers or themselves about AI use. WalkMe’s most recent AI Pulse Survey showed 32.5 percent of workers have passed AI work off as their own, and 28.3 percent have pretended to know AI in a meeting. An improvement over 2025, but still some way to go. Unsurprisingly, this lack of official approval or control is creating big risks for companies, not least in terms of data privacy and governance. The upshot is that many organizations are slowing their rate of agentic AI adoption until they are in a position to see, mitigate and reduce such risks. Traversing murky waters A second challenge many organizations face, meanwhile, is the actual cost of implementing agentic AI versus its real-world benefits. A key issue here is the underlying assumptions that many proposed financial gains are based on. These include boosting productivity and cutting headcount when the real benefits may actually be found in enhancing work quality and augmenting human activity. A third consideration is AI tokens. The problem here is that many organizations do not know either the number of tokens they are consuming or what they cost, which "can become very expensive". "So, there are many murky waters, which make it very difficult to get a real hard return on investment at this point because of all the moving parts and uncertainties," Hatsor says. The situation is made even more tricky by the sheer amount and speed of change that AI is generating. This is especially true among employees who usually have less access to new tools than their leaders and tend to be slower technology adopters anyway. Many are also fearful about a future that feels uncertain. Unsurprisingly then, according to the WalkMe report, there is a huge chasm between leaders who believe employees have been given access to adequate tooling (88 percent) compared with employees who take the same view (21 percent). This situation is inevitably hitting adoption. As Hatsor points out: "We're not giving our workforce the tools, or the confidence to use the tools, but there's also a lack of understanding of the difference between training and adoption. We can train someone to use a tool, but unless we help them adopt it and make it their own, they won't use it effectively." The power of Digital Adoption Platforms This is where systems, such as WalkMe's Digital Adoption Platform (DAP), come in. DAP offers in-app guidance - in a similar fashion to GPS systems - to navigate employees through a specific workflow. It offers information in a range of formats based on individual preferences, such as walk-through demonstrations, long-form text, or video. To discover how to create a quote in a system of record, for example, they simply open WalkMe’s action bar and view a video or PDF of how to complete the task. The system can even automate certain tasks. So, if for instance a salesperson is required to write a report confirming a particular deal, they could use WalkMe’s action bar to check the suitability of what they had written for compliance purposes and even suggest better wording, if appropriate. The key benefits of such an approach, Hatsor says, are that: "People feel supported. They also feel guided because when you're sitting in front of the screen, one of the worst things is not knowing what to do next, so we help with that." Having such support and guidance also leads to greater trust in the agentic AI system being deployed too. For instance, the WalkMe study indicates that workers who receive in-flow contextual support are 1.9 to 3.7 times more likely to feel confidence in such systems compared to those not receiving it. A huge 79 percent also say it helps them complete their work more easily. Linking business strategy and people What this demonstrates then, believes Hatsor, is just how important it is that "every agentic AI process starts with the people it's supposed to serve." But another vital consideration is ensuring a sound governance structure is in place. This is imperative as clear guardrails ensure everything, and everyone, operates safely and smoothly. This again is where WalkMe's DAP comes in. Therefore, Hatsor says: "The platform is completely secure in the sense we don't track users, we track usage, so we can see someone is interacting with a specific system, but we don't know who it is. This is important in supporting enterprise customers in terms of governance, regulation, and security." Ultimately though, WalkMe's DAP makes it possible to deploy agentic AI in a way that supports organizations' overall business strategy. It does so by clearly linking this strategy to how the technology is adopted and used by the workforce - an approach that is crucial in enabling business success. "Ignoring the human factor is a grave mistake in my view and will have an impact on the business if organizations do it. But WalkMe is one of the few pieces of technology ever developed with the sole aim of helping humans interact with enterprise IT systems - and that's the big benefit," Hatsor concludes. Sponsored by WalkMe
c317c686d9e51e1b: SHAH ALAM: A babysitter who kicked a four-year-old boy hard enough to fracture his thigh bone has failed in her bid to overturn her conviction and five-year jail sentence.
The High Court here dismissed Nurdiana Lanonming's appeal after finding that the prosecution had proven beyond reasonable doubt that she abused the child while he was under her care in June 2023.

Judge Adlin Abdul Majid also dismissed the prosecution's appeal for a heavier sentence, ruling that the five-year prison term imposed by the Kajang Sessions Court was neither too harsh nor too lenient.

In her grounds of judgment dated Oct 7, Adlin said the boy, who was four years and 11 months old at the time, was particularly vulnerable and depended entirely on Nurdiana for his safety and protection.
"At such a young age, the victim did not have the physical ability to defend himself, the maturity to understand what was happening to him or the means to seek help on his own.
"While under the accused's care, the victim depended entirely on her for his protection, safety and welfare," she said.
She said Nurdiana had betrayed the trust placed in her by the boy's parents, who had entrusted their son to her care.
"Parents who entrust their children to the care of others do so with complete trust that their children will be well looked after and protected from harm.
"This trust is a responsibility. Those entrusted with it are duty-bound to act in the best interests of the child and must never become the source of harm to them.

"Unfortunately, the accused failed to fulfil this responsibility and trust. Instead, she betrayed the trust placed in her as a caregiver by injuring the victim, a child whom she was supposed to protect," she said.
The judge said such a betrayal of trust by a caregiver was a serious aggravating factor when determining an appropriate sentence.

Adlin also rejected Nurdiana's argument that there were inconsistencies in the victim's testimony, particularly during an interview conducted at the Child Interview Centre (CIC) about two months after the incident.
She said courts could not expect young children to give evidence with the same precision, fluency and structure as adults.

"A child's failure, at such a young age, to answer certain questions during an interview, whether due to shyness, fear, confusion or an inability to understand the questions, is something that can reasonably be expected.
"It does not, in itself, cast doubt on the child's testimony," she said.
According to the facts of the case, the boy's mother sent him to Nurdiana's house at about 6.20am on June 20, 2023.
He was healthy and able to walk normally when he arrived.
However, at about 10.51am, Nurdiana called the mother to inform her that the boy's right leg was swollen and that he could no longer walk.
The mother rushed to the house and took her son to Hospital Kajang, where doctors discovered a fracture of his right femur.

On the sentence, Adlin said the court had considered Nurdiana's lack of previous criminal convictions but found that this mitigating factor had to be weighed against the seriousness of the offence and the breach of trust involved.
"The five-year prison sentence, together with the other punishments imposed by the Sessions Court, is reasonable and reflects the seriousness of the offence committed by the accused.
"The sentence is neither manifestly excessive nor manifestly inadequate. Therefore, there is no reason for this court to interfere with the sentences imposed," she added.
Deputy public prosecutor Maizatul Munirah Abdul Rahman appeared for the prosecution, while Wan M. Razali Wan A. Kadir represented Nurdiana.

0a26e540e84a2bca: KUALA LUMPUR: Gerak Khas 2.0 actress Tisha Shamsir has issued a public apology to prominent producer Datuk Yusof Haslam, acknowledging that her involvement in an ongoing drug case has damaged his reputation.

Speaking outside the Kuala Lumpur Magistrate's Court following a case mention today, the 40-year-old actress — whose real name is Shanorbiah Shamsir Alam — expressed her deep remorse and asked for strength during this difficult time, Harian Metro reported.
"I want to apologise," she said. "I know this has, to some extent, tarnished the good name of my employer, Datuk Yusof Haslam. I am also deeply sorry to my family. I am praying for the best."
She added: "This is a heavy burden, but I accept it with an open heart and hope to stay strong."
The former Mentor Season 6 contestant admitted that the legal battle has disrupted her acting career and drawn harsh criticism online.
She urged the public not to judge her before all the facts are clear.
"It is normal for people to react. If ordinary people face criticism, someone in my position will naturally face even more.
"At the end of the day, we are all human, and none of us is immune to making mistakes.
"All I ask is that people on social media do not jump to conclusions so quickly," she said.
The court has scheduled Nov 10 for the next mention of the case.
Tisha was arrested alongside several others in early July during an 'Op Noda' vice raid conducted by the police in Kuala Lumpur.
d2be29eb26a2008b: KUALA LUMPUR: National Sports Day will go ahead as planned on Saturday, but poor air quality could force changes to some activities, including possible postponements.
Youth and Sports Minister Dr Taufiq Johari said organisers were closely monitoring the Air Pollutant Index (API) and would make a decision based on advice from relevant agencies.

"We are holding regular meetings with the Ministry of Youth and Sports through the National Youth and Sports Department, along with NADMA, MET Malaysia, and related agencies to assess current API levels.
"As of today, we are still proceeding with National Sports Day. However, we must also consider the advice and views from the committee that meets daily.

"If conditions do not permit on that day, contingency measures must be considered, such as outdoor programmes, Fun Walks, or runs," Taufiq said after launching Season 2 of the Jaguh Rakan Muda reality programme at Menara KBS in Putrajaya on Thursday.

He said logistical preparations for the National Sports Day programme, including the Larian Ria MADANI at the National Stadium in Bukit Jalil on Saturday, were almost 100 per cent complete, with programme scheduling also finalised.
Taufiq stressed that public safety remained the priority, particularly with the prevailing air quality and weather conditions.

"We want to ensure that members of the public attending National Sports Day do not face health risks. We also do not encourage young children or minors to participate in any outdoor activities, Fun Walks, or Fun Runs organised at present," he said.

He added that the ministry would continue monitoring weather and API conditions over the coming days while coordinating with state executive councillors, particularly in states such as Johor where API readings were high.
"If conditions do not permit, there may need to be postponements in certain areas," he said.
Taufiq said an official announcement would be made if activities in affected states had to be postponed, stressing that no decision had been made as of Thursday.
"There will be another meeting this afternoon to ensure everything remains safe and healthy," he said.
95b0d7c811325ea5: PUTRAJAYA: Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said Malaysia was ready to facilitate efforts towards lasting peace in Myanmar.
He said this after leading Malaysia's delegation at a bilateral meeting with Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing, who is on an official visit to Malaysia.

"I stressed the importance of inclusive dialogue to make peace and reconciliation efforts in Myanmar a success, and expressed Malaysia's readiness to facilitate the process towards lasting peace," he said in a Facebook post.
Anwar said the discussions covered trade, the economy, energy and security, as well as efforts to tackle cross-border crime, which he said required coordination and shared commitment.
He said the well-being of the people had to be the priority.
"The welfare of the people must be a priority, particularly the protection of civilians and safe access to humanitarian aid for all affected communities," he said.
The repatriation of Myanmar nationals was also discussed, with an emphasis that it be carried out voluntarily, safely and with dignity, he said.

Anwar said Malaysia, guided by Madani diplomacy, would make full use of available mechanisms and channels, including through Asean, to strengthen bilateral relations and turn the understanding into concrete action.
"This is for the peace of Myanmar, the well-being of the people and shared prosperity in the region," he said.
dd756035d408d2e3: ISKANDAR PUTERI: Port of Tanjung Pelepas (PTP) is betting on electrification and green bunkering to cut emissions while strengthening its position as a major regional transshipment hub, as it deployed 52 electric prime movers in a major step towards decarbonising port operations.

Transport Minister Anthony Loke said decarbonisation was both an international obligation and a business imperative as the maritime industry moves towards the International Maritime Organisation's net-zero emissions target by 2050.
He said Malaysia also saw an opportunity to position its ports as green bunkering hubs as global shipping lines explored alternative fuels such as methanol, ammonia and liquefied natural gas.
"It's not only the ship, but at the port operations level, it is also important to reduce emissions," Loke said at the launch of PTP's complete electric prime mover fleet here today.
PTP is the first port in the country to deploy electric prime movers when 21 units entered service in August. The fleet has now expanded to 52 units.

Loke said the transition from diesel-powered equipment to electric prime movers would cut emissions from port operations, while stronger environmental, social and governance (ESG) performance would increasingly influence the competitiveness of ports.
"It's very important that we take the responsibility make our ports ESG compliance.
"When your ports achieve a certain level of ESG, that will of course give you better services, and better rankings in terms of the competitiveness of the port," he said.

He said the transport ministry's role was to establish policies and regulations to support the transition, including a regulatory roadmap for green bunkering being developed with the Australian government.

Loke said PTP's investment in the electric fleet was borne by the port operator and other port operators would need to follow as ESG requirements became increasingly important to international businesses.
PTP handled more than 14 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) in 2025 and is targeting 16 million TEUs annually by 2029.
Loke said the PTP and Johor Port, ranked 11th among the world's busiest ports in the latest Lloyd's List ranking, behind Port Klang at 10th.
"PTP's scale and transshipment role also positioned Johor to attract more investment and develop a green bunkering ecosystem," he said.
642b194da5301dad: KUALA LUMPUR: The Malaysia SEA Games Organising Committee (MASOC) is stepping up its oversight of preparations for the 2027 SEA Games to ensure spending and hosting arrangements remain within approved budgets and follow proper governance.

Youth and Sports Minister Dr Taufiq Johari said the organising committee was closely monitoring preparations as Malaysia enters the final year before hosting the biennial Games, with MASOC meeting regularly to ensure all processes run smoothly.

He was responding to concerns over financial management during the 2017 SEA Games, when an external audit conducted in 2019 uncovered several issues, including a RM9.56 million payment to a third-party vendor that was made without approval from the finance committee.

"Correct. Regarding SEA Games 2027, we are within the established timeline. Recently, we launched the 365-day or one-year countdown for SEA Games 2027," Taufiq said after launching Season 2 of the Jaguh Rakan Muda reality programme at Menara KBS in Putrajaya on Thursday.
"The MASOC meets regularly to ensure every process runs smoothly and well, adhering to proper governance and remaining within the set costs and budget."

Taufiq said the ministry wanted all hosting arrangements and implementation to comply with existing guidelines while ensuring that the focus of the Games extended beyond Malaysia's performance on the field.
"We want to make sure that all hosting arrangements and implementations follow existing guidelines and good governance.

"We also want to ensure that the SEA Games is not just about how many gold medals we can win or how prepared our athletes are. While that is very important, the overall hosting of the event is equally important," he said.

He said preparations would also focus on ensuring the opening ceremony, competition period and closing ceremony were delivered smoothly, drawing on Malaysia's experience in hosting major sporting events.

Taufiq added that the ministry would maintain close coordination with the state clusters involved in the Games — Sarawak, Johor, Penang and Kuala Lumpur — to ensure preparations remained orderly and on track.
He also said the government's allocation for sports in the 2027 Budget, to be announced by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim on Friday, would cover several areas.
"I can say our main budget focus is on sports development, athlete development, ensuring athlete welfare, youth Not in Employment, Education and Training (NEET), and youth skills," he said.
04c4568266c1882a: KUALA LUMPUR: Amendments to the Food Act 1983 are necessary to strengthen food safety controls and protect the public's right to safe food.
Health Minister Datuk Seri Dr Dzulkefly Ahmad said existing provisions under the Act were no longer sufficient to address current food safety challenges and protect public health.
"The government faces various challenges in ensuring food safety in the country.
"Among the challenges are chemical contamination, including the misuse of pesticide and antibiotic residues, as well as the excessive use of food additives.

"The government also needs to strengthen its ability to detect emerging chemicals and pathogens influenced by climate change, as well as novel foods that require more comprehensive and up-to-date risk assessments," he said while tabling the Food Act amendment Bill for its second reading in the Dewan Rakyat today.
Dzulkefly said the increasingly complex food supply chain, involving multiple stages from farm to table, also posed challenges in ensuring food safety.
He said the amendments reflected the government's commitment to strengthening controls under the Act, including provisions on definitions, regulatory powers, enforcement and penalties.

"Among the proposed changes are stronger controls over food-contact materials and expanded powers for the health director-general to close premises that prepare, store or sell food that poses a health risk.
"The amendments would also empower the director-general to make public announcements without a court order and conduct field verification of overseas food facilities," he said.

Dzulkefly said other proposed changes included regulating the entry of food intended for sale but declared for personal use, revising and standardising definitions and the director-general's powers, as well as increasing fines and the maximum prison term.
He said the amendments would also strengthen enforcement activities by clarifying and enhancing enforcement powers.

According to the Bill, the amendments include Section 3 of Act 281, enabling the minister to authorise any public officer to obtain samples of food-contact materials that could affect consumers' public interest.
Clause 4 seeks to address advertising issues and empower authorised officers to summon any person with knowledge of the facts and circumstances of a case.

Meanwhile, Clause 9 seeks to introduce a new Section 8A into Act 281, empowering authorised officers to access recorded information, computerised data or digital data to conduct thorough investigations in line with the growth of online transactions.
Clause 13 aims to introduce a new Section 11A into Act 281 to provide for the closure of premises used to prepare or sell food containing substances harmful to health.
Other amendments include Sections 15 and 16, which respectively address labelling that fails to meet food standards and false labelling, to ensure they also cover food-contact materials.
e3f05097afafa46b: KOTA KINABALU: Noraidah Lamat told the Coroner's Court today that she hoped her daughter, Zara Qairina Mahathir, would regain consciousness and tell her what had happened to her.
Noraidah said she spent the night alone with Zara at the hospital, wondering what had happened after seeing blood on her daughter's head and legs.
"It was not about spending the night with Zara. I was more concerned about her condition.
"What actually happened? Why was Zara's head bleeding? Why were Zara's legs bleeding? Who did this to her?
"I really hoped Zara would regain consciousness, open her eyes and be able to tell me what actually happened to her," she said in response to questions from lawyer Shahlan Jufri.
Noraidah, the 82nd witness, was continuing her testimony before Coroner Amir Shah Amir Hassan.
She said she stayed with Zara overnight at the hospital after her daughter was transferred to the neurological ward on the 10th floor.
The following morning, at 7am, a group of about three doctors made their rounds in the ward, accompanied by other medical officers.
She said the group included doctors she described as Chinese and Indian.
One of the doctors also offered words of encouragement that meant a great deal to her.
"The doctor said, 'Madam, you should make a police report about what happened to your daughter.'
"I asked again, 'Do I need to make a police report, doctor?'
"The doctor said, 'Make a police report for a case like this. Whether it takes a short or long time, we just have to wait for the outcome. It will take time,'" she said.
Noraidah said the doctor's words encouraged her to stay strong and keep fighting.
"Those words really encouraged me to stay strong and keep fighting," she said, describing the female doctor as relatively young and Chinese based on her facial features.
Zara was found unconscious on the ground floor of her school hostel on July 16, 2025.
She was pronounced dead the following day at Queen Elizabeth Hospital.
Her remains were exhumed on Aug 9, 2025, before a post-mortem examination was conducted the following day at the Forensic Medicine Department of Queen Elizabeth Hospital.
On Aug 20, 2025, five minors, identified by the pseudonyms Students A, B, C, D and E, were charged in the Court for Children with insulting Zara.
All five pleaded not guilty, and the trial is ongoing.

a21c07d3b7864c38: BUTTERWORTH: Three friends were fined a total of RM24,000 by the magistrate's court today after pleading guilty to threatening to kill a man and injuring his brother with sharp weapons last month.
Magistrate Aini Adilah Muhammad Faizal ordered Asyraf Hazlami Hussin, 30, Mohamad Kamarudin Hasan, 36, and Muhamad Muzzamir Bokhari, 36, to pay RM8,000 each after they admitted to two charges.

For the first charge, the trio were jointly accused of criminally intimidating Mohd Kufuan Aliff Ishak, 39, by holding a knife to his neck and threatening to kill him at Jalan Padang Benggali, Telok Air Tawar, at 10.15am on Sept 22.
The offence under Section 506 of the Penal Code, read together with Section 34, carries a maximum seven-year jail term, a fine, or both upon conviction.
The court fined each accused RM4,000 for the offence, or 10 months' imprisonment in default.
For the second charge, the three were accused of voluntarily causing hurt to Mohd Kufuan Aliff's younger brother, Mohd Rosmyzal Fammy Ishak, 36, using a parang at the same time and place.
The charge under Section 324 of the Penal Code, read together with Section 34, provides for up to 10 years' imprisonment, a fine, whipping, or any two of the punishments upon conviction.
The court fined each accused another RM4,000 for the second charge, or 12 months' imprisonment in default.
Deputy public prosecutor Siti Nurfatin Fatini Shaiful Kamarul prosecuted, while National Legal Aid Foundation lawyer Anas Hakimi Mat@Ahmad represented the accused.
In mitigation, Anas Hakimi asked for fines, saying the guilty pleas had saved court time and public funds.
He said Asyraf was single and worked at a clothing shop without a fixed income, while Kamarudin, a divorcee, worked as an excavator operator earning RM1,500 a month.
Muzzamir, also a divorcee, supported two children and earned RM1,500 monthly as a mechanic.
According to the facts of the case, the victims were in a car when the trio blocked their vehicle and approached them armed with sharp weapons.
One of the accused held a knife to Kufuan's neck, while another swung a parang at Rosmyzal, injuring his left arm.
The accused and the victims knew each other, and the incident stemmed from a misunderstanding.

Milk Diapers is a good example of building from zero to one, we helped grow the business from nothing to millions in revenue within a year, building the inventory, fulfillment and channel operations needed to support that scale. Leong sees an opportunity for Malaysian companies to build these capabilities and serve brands across the region. a72f7cda2711ac38: The ALBATROSS, a sailboat drone prototype developed by researchers at Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD), lacks the aerial grace of its avian namesake. It doesn't so much fly as plummet – an unsettling start to a sea launch, more so because it's designed to spin like a maple leaf seed as it descends. The sailboat drone's rotation slows its fall and minimizes its impact with the water. This eliminates the engineering challenge of implementing hardware for two modes of mobility. There's no need for landing gear, actuators, or sensors to manage both flying and floating. Watch and download graphics and videos of ALBATROSS here. Developed by SUTD researchers Shane Kyi Hla Win, Danial Sufiyan, Brian Leonard Suhadi, Luke Soe Thura, Xinyu Cai, Wei Jun Ang, and Shaohui Foong, the ALBATROSS represents an achievement in both acronym construction and engineering. The Airborne Lander with Buoyant AuToROtating Sailing Sensor is described in a Science paper as a hybrid robotic system that combines a bio-inspired design for controlled aerial descent with autonomous sailing. Beyond the bio-inspired operation of the rigid wingsails for creating aerodynamic lift during descent and propulsion on the water, the ALBATROSS further cribs from nature's bag of tricks with a rudder that acts like a caudal fin – it moves side to side like a tailfin to generate thrust. And it does so with just three actuators and three primary sensors. Practically, the boat drone, which weights 1.107 kg, was built to fill the gap between expendable aircraft-deployed ocean instruments and floating robots deployed from ships or shore. Its light weight and adaptability make it well suited for rapid aerial deployment followed by energy-efficient persistence on the water, as might be required to monitor an oil spill or time-sensitive weather events. It is intended to be an alternative to large automated sailboats like Saildrone and Sailbuoy that may require ground- or ship-based management. And it has far greater deployment range than hybrid aquatic micro aerial vehicles: more than 100 km, compared to about 7 km for SailMAV, or so its makers claim. "Building on prior work on guided autorotation, ALBATROSS is designed to be released from an aircraft or UAV, passively enter autorotation for a controlled, low-impact water landing, self-right without actuation, and seamlessly transition into a wind-powered sailboat," the researchers explain. "Unlike many hybrid aerial-marine systems, ALBATROSS eliminates the need for aerial propulsion, complex mechanical reconfiguration, or active stabilization during the air-water transition and can sail back to shore at the end of a mission." The prototype takes flight amid a market doing the same. Last year, PwC's Strategy& consultancy issued a report [PDF] that forecasts a sea drone market worth €18.9 billion (~$21.2 billion) by 2030, based on a compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) of 15.5 percent. By the end of the decade, most of that (84 percent) is expected to be for civilian uses like scientific research, commercial, recreational, and engineering applications, and search and rescue operations. ®
f0f07e3065fc597d: BERLIN: Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) will launch a joint motion with the small far-left BSW party in a regional parliament calling for an end to military support for Ukraine, an AfD spokesperson said on Wednesday.

The motion, to be debated in the state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt next week, will have no immediate impact on Germany's foreign policy, which is exclusively the responsibility of the federal government in Berlin.

But it underscores the AfD's strong push for an end to German support for Ukraine and a restoration of ties with Russia, which have been largely severed since Russian forces launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
"This motion symbolises the desire for change," Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD leader in Saxony-Anhalt, said in a statement.

Siegmund led the anti-immigration AfD to its best-ever election result last month, topping the state election in Saxony-Anhalt but falling just short of the majority he would need to form the first-ever AfD government.
He has since been exploring potential cooperation arrangements with the BSW, which like the AfD has long opposed German support for Ukraine.

Siegmund said the party would use every opportunity to press the government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz "to finally campaign for an end to the war rather than its prolongation" and to use the money spent in Ukraine "for the people in our country."
In a message on the social media platform X, BSW founder Sahra Wagenknecht said Germany needed "a federal government that finally makes an effort to resume dialogue with Moscow."

The motion comes some two weeks after German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul spoke to his Russian counterpart Sergei Lavrov on the margins of the United Nations General Assembly in New York at a meeting that yielded no sign of any progress.

Lavrov was dismissive about the meeting in a press conference afterwards. Germany's Foreign Ministry said the meeting had reinforced Berlin's conviction that Moscow remains unwilling to negotiate either a ceasefire or an end to the war in Ukraine.

Merz visited Kyiv at the weekend to reaffirm Berlin's support for Ukraine, while German authorities have accused Russia of carrying out a series of hybrid and drone attacks in Germany, something that Moscow denies.
46ff4d9f5e6f34cc: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's partnerships with production companies from Australia and South Korea are set to boost the local film industry through joint projects, shared expertise and direct access to global markets.
Iskandar Malaysia Studios (IMS) chief executive officer Rashid Karim said Malaysia already has an official co-production agreement with Australia.
This allows joint projects to tap government funding in both countries and qualify as local content.
He added that teaming up with South Korea offers a great chance to learn from their technical expertise and expand in regional markets.
"South Korea's creative content industry is worth over US$113 billion, so working alongside key players is a massive opportunity for our local industry," he said in a recent Bernama report.

This follows confirmation from Deputy Economy Minister Akmal Nasrullah Mohd Nasir that joint productions between Malaysian firms and Australian and South Korean partners — worth a total of US$22 million — will roll out over the next two years.
Led by OMG Studios, the partnership brings together Australia's Madman Entertainment and South Korea's Greenpatch Studio.
The deal covers two main projects: a US$10 million film and TV production with Australia, and a US$12 million feature film with South Korea.
Rashid noted that these international ventures give Johor a bigger role in the regional production landscape, thanks to IMS's facilities and the state's strategic location.
Around 60 per cent of the projects hosted at IMS this year come from overseas, mainly from the United States, Singapore and China.
Rashid said international studios choose Johor because of competitive costs, financial perks via the Film in Malaysia Incentive, world-class facilities and a wide variety of filming locations.
"Johor's proximity to Singapore, along with a skilled local crew fluent in both English and Mandarin, gives us a real competitive edge," he added.
f5b36819663871e9: KUALA LUMPUR: In a rapidly evolving digital landscape, true market leadership belongs to companies that can convert complex innovation into measurable business value. "We never just sell technology — anyone on the street can sell software," notes its chief executive, Yew Lip Sin. This focus on business impact is clearly demonstrated in their client achievements.

In one notable case study for a manufacturing client, SRKK AI modernised a legacy on-premises data setup into a scalable Microsoft Cloud architecture. The results were dramatic: processing time for critical research and development insights plummeted from 24 hours to just one hour — a 96 per cent operational efficiency gain — while saving the client over RM500,000 annually.

Serving mid-to-large corporate clients across manufacturing, logistics, retail, energy, and financial services, SRKK AI distinguishes itself through a holistic, end-to-end framework. Rather than offering isolated data or IT tools, the company integrates AI natively across every operational layer, including infrastructure, cybersecurity, ERP systems, and low-code applications.
SRKK AI is a strong proponent of digital adoption because avoiding it will result in higher implementation costs. In today's competitive economy, hesitation risks being left behind.
While targeted investments in intelligent automation allow businesses of all sizes to innovate, scale, and maintain long-term agility.

Fresh off its successful public listing, SRKK AI is accelerating its growth trajectory. The firm is currently working toward becoming an elite Microsoft Frontier Partner, certified to deploy specialised transformation engineering for advanced enterprise AI projects. By combining deep technical expertise with a commitment to ecosystem growth alongside industry bodies like PIKOM, SRKK AI is solidifying its position as a trusted driver of Southeast Asia's digital economy.
Our client achieved a 96 per cent operational efficiency gain while saving over RM500,000 annually.
f2a103a3eb7f7eca: KUALA LUMPUR: The Attorney-General's Chambers (A-GC) today returned the investigation paper on the incident at Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA) Terminal 1 to the police.

Attorney-General Tan Sri Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar confirmed that the move was to enable further investigation into the incident involving Malaysia Border Control and Protection Agency (AKPS) director-general Datuk Seri Mohd Shuhaily Mohd Zain.
He said among the aspects requiring review was the authenticity of closed-circuit television (CCTV) footage, along with several other related matters, before any decision could be finalised.
"After reviewing the investigation paper, several aspects require further investigation to complete the file.
"The investigation paper will be returned to the police today for that purpose.
"This includes verifying the authenticity of the CCTV recording and other relevant matters to complete the case investigation," he said when contacted today.
e056cc8003bbf9a2: KUALA LUMPUR: At the PIKOM Digital Excellence Awards 2026 (PDEA 2026), Cardtrend Systems Sdn Bhd secured a landmark double victory, taking home the Global Champion (Transaction Platform) award alongside the Tech Entrepreneur category for its chief executive Derek Mok.
While prestigious, this recognition represents far more than silverware — it validates a decades-long commitment to quiet, disciplined technical excellence within Malaysia's technology ecosystem.

Cardtrend operates in a vital, high-stakes segment of the digital economy: building the underlying infrastructure that captures, secures, and structures complex business-to-business (B2B) transactions. From powering large-scale fuel retail networks and government subsidy schemes to handling multi-layer corporate fleet authorizations, Cardtrend's platforms manage the complete transaction journey, encompassing authorization, business rule enforcement, reconciliation, and financial settlement.

What sets Cardtrend apart in a crowded fintech landscape is its focus on the deeper operational context behind every digital payment. Rather than simply moving funds, its proprietary software captures identities, product entitlements, limits, and settlement relationships. This creates tested, highly auditable data that allows enterprise clients to automate complex workflows and unlock meaningful strategic analytics. Investing heavily in proprietary intellectual property despite long enterprise sales cycles was once a calculated risk; today, it forms the foundation of the firm's global competitive advantage.

This dual victory at PDEA 2026 serves as a compelling case study for Malaysia's broader technology ecosystem. It demonstrates how homegrown companies can develop world-class intellectual property, navigate stringent international security standards, and compete successfully across demanding markets in Europe and Southeast Asia.

For Derek Mok and the Cardtrend team, international expansion was never an afterthought — it was a baseline ambition from day one. Their success highlights a vital evolution for Malaysia's tech landscape: moving away from operating primarily as a regional delivery hub and transforming into a true creator and exporter of high-value intellectual property. Supported by a multilingual, globally aligned workforce, Cardtrend proves that Malaysian technical talent can comfortably lead on the world stage.

As Cardtrend embarks on its next phase of international growth, its trajectory offers a clear message to the wider tech community: sustainable enterprise value is built on deep domain expertise, proprietary technology, and the confidence to take local innovations global.
6e45cedf841cd948: KUALA LUMPUR: Pentech Solution Sdn Bhd is stepping up its expansion into artificial intelligence (AI), cybersecurity and regional markets as it builds on two decades of growth in Malaysia.
The information technology solutions provider, which started operations in 2006 with 15 employees, has grown to nearly 150 employees.
It now has offices in Penang and Kuala Lumpur, and serves multinational, Malaysian and overseas customers.

Pentech Solution chief technology officer Darren Lim said the company's recognition at the PIKOM Digital Excellence Awards, where it won awards for Cloud Transformation and Managed Services, came at an important time as the company marked its 20th anniversary.
Pentech Solution Won Awards for Cloud Transformation and Managed Services
Lim said the recognition reflected the company's long-term efforts to build capabilities in cloud transformation and managed services, while earning customers' trust over the years.
Change quote to "Celebrating 20 years since Pentech" began operations in 2006 reflects how far we have come and what we have achieved.
Achieving ISO 27001 certification at the beginning of the year further demonstrates our commitment to internationally recognised standards.

"Our parent company Pentech Holdings Bhd's listing on the Ace Market in June made the occasion even more meaningful. Together, these milestones reflect our progress and position us for the next phase of growth," Lim told Business Times.
From traditional IT to cloud
Lim said, Pentech Solution began its cloud transformation journey in 2014, helping customers modernise their data centers and advance their digital transformation.

He said its managed services business provides round-the-clock support, including maintenance, preventive maintenance and proactive monitoring of customers' servers, applications, security and backup systems.
"Many customers face talent shortages and want their internal IT teams to focus on delivering business outcomes rather than day-to-day infrastructure management.

"By engaging a single vendor for services," he said. "end-to-end management and round-the-clock support, they can optimize costs, simplify accountability and free up resources for strategic priorities.
Pentech Solution has addressed this need through its managed services offering since 2020," he said.
Lim said the PIKOM awards recognised its strengths in cloud and managed services, as well as its growing AI transformation capabilities.
He said the company's ISO 27001 certification, obtained this year, assures customers that its processes, documentation, frameworks and security practices meet recognised standards.
"Customers already recognise Pentech as a trusted local company.
Our ambition is to become a world-class IT company by bringing industry best practices to customers in Malaysia," he said.
Pentech Solution has transformed from a traditional IT solutions provider into a technology business spanning cloud, AI and cybersecurity.
Drawing on that experience, the company now helps customers modernise their technology environments, adopt new capabilities and align digital transformation with business outcomes.
The company has also invested in upskilling and reskilling employees, moving some of its traditional IT workforce into areas including AI, digital transformation and cybersecurity.
Lim said the strategy was well-timed, as the Covid-19 pandemic accelerated demand for cloud technologies.
"During the Movement Control Order (MCO), everybody was working from home.
"So, whatever groundwork we had done in 2018 and 2019 started happening.
"Our growth began with cloud transformation in 2019 and accelerated significantly through 2022.
"Since then, we have expanded beyond cloud into cybersecurity, AI and managed services," he said.
Listing to fund next phase
With the business now moving further into AI and cybersecurity, Lim said the ACE Market listing was intended to provide the resources needed to transform the organisation further.
"One of the main reasons for our listing is to expand our cybersecurity business. We have acquired a new lot in Kuala Lumpur, beside our existing premise.
"We are going to establish our first local Malaysian security operations centre by a local IT solutions company," he said.
AI is another focus, although Lim said talent availability remains a challenge as customer demand increases.
He said Pentech Solution's AI strategy was focused on addressing specific customer needs rather than developing technology simply for the sake of having a product.
"Pentech Solution's AI solutions are supported by a structured process and framework designed to address customers' business challenges.
"As every industry has different AI requirements, we tailor each solution to the customer's specific needs.
"Through this framework, we help customers transform their operations and ensure that their investment in AI delivers measurable business outcomes and returns," he said.
Eyes Overseas Expansion
Beyond technology investment, Lim said Pentech Solution is also looking to expand beyond Malaysia, with Singapore emerging as a potential next market.
He said the company's multinational customers were an important factor in determining where it should expand.
"If you ask me, my next step most probably will be in Singapore because some of our existing Malaysian customers are there," he said.
Lim said the company had yet to finalise a concrete plan for Singapore, with strengthening its foundation in Malaysia remaining a priority.
He said that Pentech Solution's overseas business had already grown, with its contribution to revenue rising from about 1 per cent in 2022 to 4 per cent in 2025.
The company is managing cross-border services and strengthening relationships with existing customers as it considers potential next markets.

d12dbd05d82f46c8: KOTA KINABALU: Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim's meeting with Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing today does not constitute recognition of the country's government but is aimed at resolving the longstanding issue of Myanmar refugees in Malaysia.
Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil said the meeting reflected the government's use of diplomatic channels to address domestic concerns, particularly those involving Myanmar refugees.

"This meeting does not mean we recognise the Myanmar government. It is intended to find a solution to the longstanding issue of Myanmar refugees in our country," he said at the opening of the Inanam Sentral National Information Dissemination Centre (Nadi) here today.
Fahmi also expressed hope that the meeting would yield positive results, including facilitating the return of Myanmar refugees through proper channels.

"We hope the prime minister's meeting with the Myanmar President today will produce positive outcomes, allowing refugees from Myanmar's 19 ethnic groups in Malaysia to return to their country through proper channels and helping us address the issues we face domestically," he said.

Fahmi, who is also the government spokesperson, highlighted another important meeting scheduled for tomorrow after the tabling of the 2027 Budget, with discussions expected to cover efforts to strengthen bilateral ties and issues concerning Palestine.
"Let us await the outcomes of these two important meetings taking place today and tomorrow," he said.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi is scheduled to make a state visit to Malaysia from Oct 9 to 10.
8c3e5076a961bfeb: PONTIAN: "I told them there was no need to go because school was closed today, but they insisted.
"So their older brother took them there to show them that the school was indeed closed. But on the way home, they were involved in the accident."
Julaiha Munaji, 42, said her three children were killed in a collision involving a motorcycle and lorry at Jalan Parit Haji Sirat here this morning.
She said she had told Nor Daniel Fikri Norlizan, 11, and Puteri Naufal Raisya, 8, they did not need to go to school as all schools in Johor were closed due to the haze.

dbc01932a536b398: LETTER: The 2026 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia was awesome. Congratulations to Max Verstappen for his first win of the 2026 season despite the rain, delays and rapidly changing conditions.
Sepang did not simply host the race. It became part of the drama.
The circuit is legendary. Its long straights, fast corners and wide racing surface give drivers room to attack, while its technical sections punish mistakes.
Heat, humidity, and the ever-present threat of tropical rain added to the challenge.
Put them together, and it is a nightmare for strategists, a great challenge for drivers and pure entertainment for spectators.
That may be the simplest way to describe the weekend. A crowd that still cares
The numbers tell one part of the story. A record 261,000 spectators attended over the race weekend, with 103,000 on race day, making it the largest crowd in Sepang circuit history.
The atmosphere became a defining feature of the weekend. Fans around the world praised the Malaysian crowd, while calls for Sepang to return to the Formula 1 calendar grew louder after the race.
And that is where the significance of this unexpected Grand Prix begins. Malaysia had not returned to Formula 1 through a long-term agreement or an elaborate comeback campaign.
Conflict in the Middle East disrupted the Bahrain race, and Sepang stepped in to replace it. For us, the opportunity goes beyond motorsport.
Formula 1 is one of the world's most powerful sporting platforms. Its global audience gives the host country an opportunity to showcase itself far beyond the circuit.
Malaysia should therefore look at the 2026 race not simply through the number of spectators who attended, but through what those visitors contributed to the wider tourism economy.
Visitors attending the race stayed in hotels, used local transportation, dined at restaurants, shopped, and, in some cases, explored destinations beyond Sepang.
Meanwhile, team social media channels and drivers' visits to Malaysian destinations extended the event's reach, showcasing Malaysia to a global audience beyond the F1 paddock.
In turn, F1 can become a tourism platform that encourages longer stays, wider visitor dispersal, and greater spending across the tourism value chain.
The race has already delivered international attention. The next challenge is to determine how much of that attention can be converted into lasting tourism and economic value.
Discussions are already underway to bring F1 back to Malaysia on a more permanent basis, with Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim opening the door to further consideration of Sepang's future.
As Malaysians, we will be very proud if the race returns to the circuit. A permanent return will come with significant financial and operational commitments.
If the 2027 calendar faces disruption, Sepang could once again serve as a potential Plan B, having demonstrated its readiness and capacity this year.
Another possibility is for Formula 1 to reserve two or three "wild-card" slots each season, allowing different countries and circuits to join the calendar periodically.
